d001-garden.title: Light and the first garden
d001-garden.story: Genesis opens with the earth empty and dark, and God speaking light into being. Over six days the account moves from light to sky, from land and seas to plants, from sun, moon and stars to creatures of the water, air and ground, and last to people, made in God's image. God calls what he has made good, and the seventh day is set apart for rest. Chapter 2 then slows down to a garden in Eden, where God places the man to work it and care for it.
d001-garden.why: It frames everything that follows: the world is made on purpose and called good, and people are given a place in it with meaning.

d002-ark.title: Noah builds the ark
d002-ark.story: Genesis says the earth had filled with violence, and God told Noah to build a large ark. Noah, his family and the animals went in, and floodwaters covered the earth for a long time. When the water went down, the ark came to rest in the mountains of Ararat, and Noah sent out a raven and a dove to learn whether the ground was dry. After they left the ark, God promised never again to flood the whole earth and set a rainbow in the clouds as the sign of that promise.
d002-ark.why: The rainbow is a sign of a promise made to every living thing, a reminder in this story that mercy outlasts judgment.

d003-rainbow.title: The dove, the olive leaf and the rainbow
d003-rainbow.story: After many months the floodwater began to drop, and the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat. Noah sent out a raven and then a dove, and the second time the dove came back with a fresh olive leaf in its beak. Later the dove did not return, and God told Noah to bring everyone out of the ark. Noah built an altar, and God promised never again to flood the whole earth, setting a rainbow in the clouds as the sign.
d003-rainbow.why: The olive leaf shows that new life can start again after the worst, and the rainbow is a promise a person can see for themselves.

d004-tower_babel.title: The tower of Babel
d004-tower_babel.story: Everyone on earth once spoke one language, and the people settled on a plain in Shinar. They decided to build a city with a tower reaching the heavens so they could make a name for themselves and not be scattered. The Lord came down to see it, mixed up their language so they could no longer understand each other, and scattered them over the whole earth. The city was called Babel. The story then turns to Abram, whom God calls to leave his country and go to a land he will show him.
d004-tower_babel.why: People who build to make themselves great end up divided, while God's blessing is promised to come through one family for all the peoples of the earth.

d005-oak.title: Visitors under the oaks
d005-oak.story: Abraham was sitting at the door of his tent by the oaks of Mamre when three visitors came by. He hurried to welcome them, and Sarah baked bread while he prepared a meal. They told him that Sarah would have a son within the year, and Sarah laughed because they were both so old. Earlier, Hagar, who had run away into the desert, had met God at a spring and called him the God who sees me.
d005-oak.why: The story treats a plain meal for strangers as holy ground, and it says that nobody, even someone alone in the desert, goes unseen.

d005-stars.title: Visitors under the oaks
d005-stars.story: Abraham was sitting at the door of his tent by the oaks of Mamre when three visitors came by. He hurried to welcome them, and Sarah baked bread while he prepared a meal. They told him that Sarah would have a son within the year, and Sarah laughed because they were both so old. Earlier, Hagar, who had run away into the desert, had met God at a spring and called him the God who sees me.
d005-stars.why: The story treats a plain meal for strangers as holy ground, and it says that nobody, even someone alone in the desert, goes unseen.

d006-ruins.title: Smoke over Sodom
d006-ruins.story: Two angels came to Lot in the city of Sodom, and the city's men crowded his house in a threatening way. The angels led Lot, his wife and his two daughters out and told them to flee and not look back. Fire fell on Sodom and the cities nearby, and Lot's wife looked back and was lost. Abraham, who had pleaded earlier for the city, saw smoke rising from the valley the next morning.
d006-ruins.why: It is a sober chapter that shows a rescue in the middle of judgment, and that God hears the prayers of a person who pleads for others.

d007-altar.title: Abraham's altar on Moriah
d007-altar.story: God told Abraham to take his son Isaac to a mountain in the region of Moriah and offer him there. Abraham went, built the altar and laid out the wood, and Isaac asked where the lamb was. Abraham said God would provide it. Just as he lifted his hand, an angel called him to stop, and Abraham saw a ram caught in a bush and offered that instead.
d007-altar.why: The account says that God provides, and Abraham named the place for that: on the mountain of the Lord it will be provided.

d007-well.title: Abraham's altar on Moriah
d007-well.story: God told Abraham to take his son Isaac to a mountain in the region of Moriah and offer him there. Abraham went, built the altar and laid out the wood, and Isaac asked where the lamb was. Abraham said God would provide it. Just as he lifted his hand, an angel called him to stop, and Abraham saw a ram caught in a bush and offered that instead.
d007-well.why: The account says that God provides, and Abraham named the place for that: on the mountain of the Lord it will be provided.

d008-tent_camp.title: Esau sells his birthright
d008-tent_camp.story: Rebekah gave birth to twin sons, Esau, who was red and hairy, and Jacob, who came out holding his brother's heel. Esau grew up to be a skilled hunter, and Jacob was a quiet man who stayed among the tents. One day Esau came in from the field faint with hunger and asked Jacob for some of the red stew he was cooking. Jacob made him swear to sell his birthright first, and Esau ate and drank and went on his way, treating the birthright as worth little.
d008-tent_camp.why: Esau gave away something lasting to ease the hunger of one moment, a reminder to weigh what we trade away for what we want right now.

d009-well.title: Isaac digs the wells again
d009-well.story: A famine came and Isaac settled among the Philistines in Gerar, where God made his crops and flocks grow. The Philistines had filled his father's wells with earth, so Isaac dug them again and gave them the old names. When herdsmen quarreled over a new well, he moved on rather than fight. At the third well no one argued, and he named it Rehoboth, which means room, saying that now the Lord had given them room.
d009-well.why: The story rewards patience over a fight, and the quiet person who keeps digging finds room in the end.

d010-ladder.title: Jacob's ladder
d010-ladder.story: Jacob was leaving home alone, running from his brother Esau's anger after taking Esau's blessing. At night he lay down with a stone for a pillow and dreamed of a stairway that reached from earth to heaven, with angels going up and down on it. God stood above it and repeated the promise made to Abraham and Isaac, adding that he would be with Jacob wherever he went. Jacob woke and said God was surely in this place, and he named it Bethel, which means house of God.
d010-ladder.why: Jacob was on the run and by himself, and the dream says God's presence meets people even there.

d010-cairn.title: Jacob's ladder
d010-cairn.story: Jacob was leaving home alone, running from his brother Esau's anger after taking Esau's blessing. At night he lay down with a stone for a pillow and dreamed of a stairway that reached from earth to heaven, with angels going up and down on it. God stood above it and repeated the promise made to Abraham and Isaac, adding that he would be with Jacob wherever he went. Jacob woke and said God was surely in this place, and he named it Bethel, which means house of God.
d010-cairn.why: Jacob was on the run and by himself, and the dream says God's presence meets people even there.

d011-stream.title: Wrestling at the Jabbok
d011-stream.story: Jacob left his uncle Laban's house with his family and flocks, and he and Laban piled up a heap of stones as a witness to the peace between them. Hearing that Esau was coming with four hundred men, Jacob prayed and then sent gifts ahead. That night, alone by the Jabbok stream, a man wrestled with him until daybreak. Jacob would not let go until he was blessed, and he was given the new name Israel, and left with a limp.
d011-stream.why: Jacob came away hurt and blessed at the same time, which is how a lot of honest struggle with God ends.

d012-tent_camp.title: Jacob and Esau reconciled
d012-tent_camp.story: Jacob bowed to the ground seven times as he approached, afraid of what Esau would do. Esau ran to meet him, hugged him and wept, and the two brothers were reconciled. Later God told Jacob to go back to Bethel. Jacob told his household to put away their foreign gods, and he buried them under an oak, then built an altar at the place where he had first met God.
d012-tent_camp.why: Jacob feared the worst, but forgiveness met him on the road, and a fresh start began with letting go of old idols.

d013-caravan.title: Joseph sold to the traders
d013-caravan.story: Jacob loved Joseph more than his other sons and gave him a richly woven coat, and his brothers grew jealous, especially after Joseph shared dreams in which they bowed to him. One day in the fields near Dothan the brothers threw him into an empty pit. When a caravan of traders passed on its way to Egypt, they sold him for twenty pieces of silver. They dipped the coat in goat's blood and showed it to Jacob, who mourned for many days.
d013-caravan.why: The story starts with a family broken by favoritism and jealousy, and it is told honestly about how much harm that can do.

d014-prison.title: Dreams in prison
d014-prison.story: In Egypt, Joseph served in the house of an official named Potiphar until he was accused of something he did not do and sent to prison. God was with him there, and the prison keeper put him in charge of the other prisoners. Two of Pharaoh's officers, the cupbearer and the baker, each had a dream that troubled them. Joseph said that interpretations belong to God, and what he said came true. The cupbearer was restored to his job but he forgot all about Joseph.
d014-prison.why: Joseph's gift kept working while he was forgotten and unfairly held, which shows that the years in the dark were not wasted.

d015-storehouse.title: Pharaoh's dreams and the storehouses
d015-storehouse.story: Pharaoh dreamed of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones, and seven full heads of grain eaten by seven withered ones. The cupbearer finally remembered Joseph, who was brought from prison. Joseph said the dreams meant seven good years followed by seven years of famine, and he told Pharaoh to store grain. Pharaoh made Joseph his second in command, and Joseph filled the storehouses across Egypt before the hunger came.
d015-storehouse.why: The story shows careful planning for a hard season and gives credit to God for the wisdom to do it.

d016-palace.title: Joseph reveals himself
d016-palace.story: When the famine reached Canaan, Joseph's brothers came to Egypt for grain and did not recognize him. He tested them, and when Judah offered to take Benjamin's place as a servant, Joseph could no longer hold back. He sent everyone else out, wept loudly, and said, I am Joseph. He told his frightened brothers not to be angry with themselves, because God had sent him ahead to save many lives, and then he invited his father to come to Egypt.
d016-palace.why: The whole account is about forgiveness, and Joseph looks back at his own pain and sees something good that God brought out of it.

d017-pyramids.title: Jacob goes down to Egypt
d017-pyramids.story: Jacob, now old, set out for Egypt with his family. At Beersheba God spoke to him in the night and told him not to be afraid to go. About seventy people from his family arrived, and Joseph came to meet his father in a chariot and held him for a long time. Pharaoh gave them the land of Goshen, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh. Joseph kept the family fed through the famine.
d017-pyramids.why: The family that nearly fell apart was reunited in a foreign land, and God's promise went with them.

d018-city_wall.title: Bricks and building in Egypt
d018-city_wall.story: Before he died, Jacob blessed Joseph's two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, and then each of his own twelve sons. After his death Joseph's brothers feared he would pay them back, but Joseph said that what they had meant for harm God had meant for good. Joseph asked that his bones be carried out of Egypt one day. Exodus then opens with a new king who did not know Joseph and forced the Israelites to make bricks and build cities.
d018-city_wall.why: It ends one story with forgiveness and starts the next with oppression, and it holds the hope of a promise still ahead.

d019-bush.title: The bush that does not burn
d019-bush.story: Moses was looking after sheep near Mount Horeb when he saw a bush that was on fire but was not burning up. As he stepped closer, God called to him from the bush and told him to take off his sandals, because the ground was holy. God said he had seen the suffering of his people in Egypt and was sending Moses to bring them out. Moses protested that he was the wrong person for the task, and God answered by promising to be with him.
d019-bush.why: God's call comes to someone who feels unqualified, and the answer is his presence, not Moses' qualifications.

d020-stream.title: The Nile runs red
d020-stream.story: Moses and Aaron asked Pharaoh to let the Israelites go into the desert to worship, but he refused and made them gather their own straw for bricks while making the same number. The people blamed Moses, and Moses took his complaint to God, who promised to bring them out. Later, when Moses and Aaron met Pharaoh by the Nile, Aaron struck the river with his staff and the water turned to blood. Pharaoh's heart stayed hard.
d020-stream.why: Freedom did not come quickly, and the story admits that things got worse before they got better.

d021-plagues.title: Frogs, hail and darkness
d021-plagues.story: More plagues fell on Egypt one after another: frogs, gnats, flies, sick animals, boils, hail, locusts and then three days of darkness so thick it could be felt. The flies, the sickness on the animals and the hail did not touch the Israelites in Goshen, and during the darkness they had light. Several times Pharaoh asked Moses to pray and promised to let the people go, then changed his mind when relief came.
d021-plagues.why: The record is about a ruler who kept trading away his own promises, and about a God who kept giving him the chance to listen.

d022-passover_door.title: The Passover night
d022-passover_door.story: Before the last plague, Moses called the elders of Israel and told them to pick out a lamb for each family and kill the Passover animal. They were to dip a bunch of hyssop in the blood and put some on the top and both sides of the doorframe, and no one was to go out of the house until morning. The Lord would pass through to strike down the firstborn of Egypt, but he would pass over every door marked with blood and not let the destroyer enter. At midnight the firstborn in Egypt died, and Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron in the night and told the Israelites to go.
d022-passover_door.why: The marked doorframe shows a night of rescue that a whole people kept remembering every year and passing on to their children.

d023-redsea.title: Through the sea
d023-redsea.story: After leaving Egypt, the people found the sea in front of them and Pharaoh's army behind them. Moses stretched out his hand, and through the night a strong east wind drove the sea back, so the Israelites crossed on dry ground with walls of water on either side. When the Egyptian army followed, the water returned and covered them. Moses and the people then sang in praise to God for the rescue, and Miriam led the women with a tambourine.
d023-redsea.why: It is the great rescue of the Old Testament, the story the people return to when they need to remember that God brings freedom.

d023-manna_quail.title: Through the sea
d023-manna_quail.story: After leaving Egypt, the people found the sea in front of them and Pharaoh's army behind them. Moses stretched out his hand, and through the night a strong east wind drove the sea back, so the Israelites crossed on dry ground with walls of water on either side. When the Egyptian army followed, the water returned and covered them. Moses and the people then sang in praise to God for the rescue, and Miriam led the women with a tambourine.
d023-manna_quail.why: It is the great rescue of the Old Testament, the story the people return to when they need to remember that God brings freedom.

d024-sinai.title: Mountain of smoke and fire
d024-sinai.story: In the third month after leaving Egypt, the people camped at the foot of Mount Sinai. God told Moses he would meet them there, and the people spent two days preparing. On the third morning there was thunder and lightning, a thick cloud and a very loud trumpet blast, and the whole mountain was wrapped in smoke because the Lord had come down on it in fire. Moses went up the mountain to speak with God.
d024-sinai.why: It is where Israel is given the law and the covenant, and where they begin to be shaped as a people who belong to God.

d024-rock_spring.title: Mountain of smoke and fire
d024-rock_spring.story: In the third month after leaving Egypt, the people camped at the foot of Mount Sinai. God told Moses he would meet them there, and the people spent two days preparing. On the third morning there was thunder and lightning, a thick cloud and a very loud trumpet blast, and the whole mountain was wrapped in smoke because the Lord had come down on it in fire. Moses went up the mountain to speak with God.
d024-rock_spring.why: It is where Israel is given the law and the covenant, and where they begin to be shaped as a people who belong to God.

d025-stone_tablets.title: The ten commandments
d025-stone_tablets.story: At Sinai, God spoke the Ten Commandments to the people. They begin with God, who brought Israel out of Egypt, and call the people to have no other gods, to make no idols or images to worship, and not to misuse God's name. They go on to keep the Sabbath day and honor father and mother, and they forbid murder, adultery, stealing, lying about a neighbor and coveting what belongs to someone else. Later in Exodus the words are written on two tablets of stone.
d025-stone_tablets.why: They are a short picture of what it means to love God and to love your neighbor, and later writers keep returning to them.

d026-covenant_chest.title: Plans for the ark of the covenant
d026-covenant_chest.story: The people agreed to keep God's covenant, and Moses sealed it with sacrifices. Aaron and seventy elders went up the mountain, saw God, and shared a meal there. Moses then went higher and stayed forty days. God gave him plans for a chest of acacia wood covered in gold, with a lid and two winged figures facing each other, a table for bread, and a golden lampstand. God said that he would meet Moses there and speak with him.
d026-covenant_chest.why: The chest was to be a meeting place, a visible sign that God would be near his people and speak with them.

d027-tabernacle.title: The tent of meeting is planned
d027-tabernacle.story: God gave Moses the plans for the tent of meeting, where he would meet with his people. The plans covered curtains of fine linen, wooden frames, a veil to divide the inner room, and a courtyard around it. Aaron and his sons were given priestly clothing, with stones engraved with the names of the twelve tribes on the shoulders and breastpiece. The whole tent could be taken down and carried.
d027-tabernacle.why: It was a portable home for God's presence, and it moved wherever the people went.

d028-altar.title: The altar and the setting apart of the priests
d028-altar.story: God gave detailed instructions for setting apart Aaron and his sons as priests, with washing, special clothes, anointing with oil and offerings over seven days. A morning and evening offering was to be made every day, and God said he would dwell among the Israelites and be their God. Moses was also told to make an altar for incense, to count the people with a half shekel for each person, and to prepare a basin for washing.
d028-altar.why: It shows that coming near to God was meant to be done with care, and that everyone, rich or poor, gave the same amount.

d029-golden_calf.title: The golden calf
d029-golden_calf.story: Moses was on the mountain a long time, and the people grew restless and asked Aaron to make them a god. Aaron collected their gold earrings and cast a calf, and the people held a feast. God told Moses what was happening, and Moses pleaded with God for them. Coming down, he broke the tablets in anger, ground up the calf and made the people face what they had done. About three thousand people died that day, and Moses went back up to ask God to forgive them.
d029-golden_calf.why: The story is honest about how quickly people give up on waiting, and it shows Moses standing in the gap for them.

d030-pillar_cloud.title: The tent outside the camp
d030-pillar_cloud.story: After the calf, Moses pitched a tent of meeting outside the camp, and whenever he went in, the pillar of cloud came down to stand at the door. The text says God spoke to Moses face to face, as one speaks to a friend. God agreed to go with them, and Moses asked to see God's glory, and after he cut two new stone tablets and carried them up the mountain, God passed by him, saying he was compassionate and gracious, slow to anger and rich in love. Later the people brought gifts for the tent.
d030-pillar_cloud.why: Even after the worst failure, God did not leave, and the closeness Moses had with him was like a friend's.

d031-lampstand.title: The lampstand and the ark made
d031-lampstand.story: The craftsmen Bezalel and Oholiab, whom God had filled with skill, began to build the tent. The people brought so many gifts that Moses had to tell them to stop. Bezalel made the ark of acacia wood covered with gold, the table for the bread, and the lampstand of pure hammered gold, shaped like a tree with branches and flowers. He also made the altars and a bronze basin for washing.
d031-lampstand.why: People gave freely until there was more than enough, and skilled hands made the plans real.

d032-tabernacle.title: The cloud fills the tent
d032-tabernacle.story: The tent was finished and the clothes for the priests were made exactly as God had directed. Moses looked over the work and blessed the people. On the first day of the new year, they set up the tent, put the ark inside, and hung the veil. Then the cloud covered the tent and the glory of the Lord filled it, so that Moses could not go in. After that, the Israelites set out on their journey only when the cloud lifted.
d032-tabernacle.why: God's presence moved with the people, and they learned to follow it step by step.

d033-altar.title: The burnt offering
d033-altar.story: Leviticus begins with God speaking to Moses from the tent and explaining how the people should bring offerings. A burnt offering, a grain offering and a fellowship offering were gifts that came from what a person had, such as a bull, a lamb, flour or doves. A person laid a hand on the animal's head. There were also offerings for wrongs done without meaning to, and the book says the person would be forgiven.
d033-altar.why: These laws take wrongdoing seriously, and they also make clear that there was a way back.

d034-firstfruits.title: Grain, fellowship and guilt offerings
d034-firstfruits.story: More offering rules follow, and some portions of the offerings were given to the priests to eat. A fellowship offering could be brought to give thanks, and its meat had to be eaten the same day. When someone cheated a neighbor or kept what was not theirs, they had to repay it in full, add a fifth more, and then bring an offering to God.
d034-firstfruits.why: The law set wrongs right with the person who was hurt first, and then made peace with God.

d035-tabernacle.title: The priests begin to serve
d035-tabernacle.story: Moses washed and dressed Aaron and his sons, anointed them with oil, and set them apart for seven days. On the eighth day Aaron made the first offerings for himself and for the people, then blessed them. Fire came out from God and burned up the offering on the altar, and the people shouted and bowed with their faces to the ground. Then two of Aaron's sons offered fire that God had not asked for, and they died, and Aaron was silent in his grief.
d035-tabernacle.why: God's welcome was joyful and his holiness was serious, and the book does not hide either.

d036-scroll.title: Clean and unclean
d036-scroll.story: God gave rules about which animals could be eaten and which could not, and about skin diseases, mold in clothes and what to do after childbirth. A priest was to look at a skin condition and, if needed, keep the person apart for seven days and look again. God said, be holy, because I am holy. The rules marked Israel as a people set apart for God.
d036-scroll.why: Many of the rules look strange now, but all of them reminded people that daily life belonged to God.

d037-oil_jars.title: Oil and water for cleansing
d037-oil_jars.story: When a person with a skin disease was healed, the priest went outside the camp to examine them. Two birds were taken, and one was set free over the open fields. The person washed, shaved, and waited seven days, then brought offerings. The priest touched oil to the person's right ear, thumb and toe. Someone who was poor could bring one lamb with two doves or young pigeons instead of three lambs.
d037-oil_jars.why: It shows a sick person welcomed back into the community, and it gave poor people a way to take part too.

d038-wilderness.title: The day of atonement
d038-wilderness.story: Aaron was to go into the inner room of the tent once a year with offerings for himself and the people. Two goats were chosen. One was offered, and Aaron laid his hands on the head of the other and confessed the people's wrongs over it. A man then led that goat away into the wilderness, carrying their wrongs far from the camp. The day was a time to fast and rest.
d038-wilderness.why: It pictured wrongs being taken away, and later readers have often drawn on it when they speak of forgiveness.

d039-harvest.title: Leave the edges of the field
d039-harvest.story: Leviticus 19 gathers many everyday commands: do not steal or lie, pay a worker the same day, do not curse someone who cannot hear, and honor older people. Farmers were told not to harvest to the very edges of their fields or pick up what fell, but to leave it for the poor and the foreigner. The chapter says to love your neighbor as yourself, and to treat the foreigner as one of your own.
d039-harvest.why: It makes love practical, since it asks for something as ordinary as leaving a bit of the harvest behind.

d040-shofar.title: The appointed feasts
d040-shofar.story: Leviticus 23 lists the festivals Israel was to keep each year. There was a weekly day of rest, Passover and the bread without yeast, the first sheaf of the harvest, and a festival of weeks. In the seventh month a trumpet was blown, then came the day of atonement and a festival of shelters, when everyone lived in huts for a week to remember the desert years.
d040-shofar.why: The calendar built remembering into the year, so that history was something the whole community acted out and celebrated.

d041-lamp.title: Lamp oil and the year of jubilee
d041-lamp.story: The lamps in the tent were to burn all night with pure olive oil, and twelve loaves of bread were set out fresh each Sabbath. Then God told Israel to let the land rest every seventh year. Every fiftieth year was the jubilee: a trumpet sounded, land went back to its original family, and people who had sold themselves into service went free. God said the land was his, and people were only his tenants.
d041-lamp.why: The jubilee was an attempt to stop a gap between rich and poor from growing forever, and it started over every fifty years.

d042-vineyard.title: Blessing on a fruitful land
d042-vineyard.story: Leviticus 26 sets out a promise: if Israel followed God's commands, there would be rain, harvests, peace and God walking among them. It also warns what would happen if they turned away, but says that even then God would remember his covenant if they came back. Chapter 27 ends the book with rules about vows, gifts to God and giving a tenth of crops and herds.
d042-vineyard.why: The offer of blessing came with a clear warning, and the door stayed open to return.

d043-tent_camp.title: The camp around the tent
d043-tent_camp.story: God told Moses to count the men of Israel who were twenty or older and able to serve in the army, tribe by tribe, and the total was over six hundred thousand. The Levites were not counted with them, because they cared for the tent. Then God told them how to camp: the tent in the middle, the Levites close around it, and three tribes on each side, each under its own banner.
d043-tent_camp.why: The camp was laid out around God's tent, with his presence at the center of everyone's day.

d044-covenant_chest.title: Carrying the ark on poles
d044-covenant_chest.story: The Levites were given to God in place of the firstborn of Israel and assigned work according to their families. The Gershonites cared for the curtains, the Merarites for the frames and posts, and the Kohathites for the holy things inside. When the camp moved, the priests covered the ark with the veil and other cloths, and the Kohathites carried it on poles. They were not allowed to touch the holy things.
d044-covenant_chest.why: Every task, from curtains to the ark, had someone assigned to it, and everything was carried with care.

d045-scroll.title: The priestly blessing
d045-scroll.story: Numbers 5 and 6 deal with keeping the camp pure, setting wrongs right, and the Nazirite vow, in which a man or woman set themselves apart for a time by avoiding wine, not cutting their hair and keeping away from the dead. The passage ends with the words God gave Aaron to say over the people: May the Lord bless you and keep you; may the Lord make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; may the Lord look on you with favor and give you peace.
d045-scroll.why: These lines are still spoken as a blessing at the end of services and gatherings, and they ask for protection, kindness and peace.

d046-treasury.title: Gifts for the altar
d046-treasury.story: When the altar was set up, the leaders of the twelve tribes each brought the same gifts: a silver plate, a silver bowl, a gold dish full of incense, and animals for the offerings. The leaders came one tribe a day for twelve days, and the text lists each gift out in full for each tribe. When Moses went into the tent, he heard God speaking from above the lid of the ark.
d046-treasury.why: Every tribe gave an equal gift, and none was left out or counted for less.

d047-shofar.title: Silver trumpets and the cloud
d047-shofar.story: The lamps were lit, the Levites were washed and set apart, and the people celebrated Passover in the desert. The cloud covered the tent by day and looked like fire at night, and the people moved only when it moved. God also told Moses to make two silver trumpets to call the people together and signal when to set out. After almost a year at Sinai, the camp set out, with the ark going ahead of them.
d047-shofar.why: They had a sign by day and night to follow, and the trumpets told the whole camp when it was time to go.

d048-manna_quail.title: Quail in the camp
d048-manna_quail.story: The people began to complain that they had no meat and missed the fish of Egypt, and Moses felt it was too heavy a load to carry alone. God gave Moses seventy elders to share the work, and a wind brought quail from the sea in huge numbers. Later Moses sent twelve men to look over Canaan. They came back with a cluster of grapes so big two men carried it on a pole, but most of them said the people there were too strong to fight.
d048-manna_quail.why: The twelve scouts saw the same land, and some saw fruit while others saw giants.

d049-wilderness.title: Fear at the border
d049-wilderness.story: The people wept all night and said they would rather go back to Egypt. Joshua and Caleb, two of the scouts, said the land was good and that God would give it to them, but the crowd talked of stoning them. Moses pleaded with God for the people, and God forgave them but said that this generation would not enter the land and the people would wander forty years. Then God told them to sew tassels on their clothes to remember his commands.
d049-wilderness.why: Fear can cost a lot, and the tassels gave people something to look at and be reminded of every day.

d050-stump_shoot.title: Aaron's staff blossoms
d050-stump_shoot.story: Korah, Dathan and Abiram challenged Moses and Aaron's right to lead, and the account says the earth opened and swallowed them and the next day a plague broke out among those who grumbled. To settle the question of who God had chosen, Moses had each tribe's leader put a staff in the tent. The next morning, Aaron's staff had sprouted, budded and produced almonds. It was put in front of the ark as a reminder.
d050-stump_shoot.why: It is a hard chapter about a leadership quarrel, and the staff is a gentle sign that settled it.

d051-serpent_pole.title: The bronze serpent
d051-serpent_pole.story: As the people traveled around Edom, they grew discouraged and spoke against God and Moses. Poisonous snakes came among them and many were bitten. The people confessed and asked Moses to pray. God told Moses to make a bronze snake and put it on a pole, and anyone who was bitten and looked at it lived. Further on, Israel won battles against the kings of the Amorites and of Bashan.
d051-serpent_pole.why: The cure was as simple as looking up, and it is a picture of how healing sometimes starts with turning toward it.

d051-rock_spring.title: The bronze serpent
d051-rock_spring.story: As the people traveled around Edom, they grew discouraged and spoke against God and Moses. Poisonous snakes came among them and many were bitten. The people confessed and asked Moses to pray. God told Moses to make a bronze snake and put it on a pole, and anyone who was bitten and looked at it lived. Further on, Israel won battles against the kings of the Amorites and of Bashan.
d051-rock_spring.why: The cure was as simple as looking up, and it is a picture of how healing sometimes starts with turning toward it.

d052-signpost.title: Balaam and the donkey
d052-signpost.story: Balak, king of Moab, was afraid of Israel and sent for a prophet named Balaam to curse them. God told Balaam to go but to say only what he was given. On the road, Balaam's donkey saw an angel with a drawn sword and turned aside, and Balaam beat her. The donkey spoke, and then Balaam's eyes were opened to see the angel. At the high places Balaam blessed Israel instead, and Balak was furious.
d052-signpost.why: A king tried to buy a curse, and the text says it was not for sale.

d053-stars.title: The star from Jacob
d053-stars.story: Balaam looked out over the camp of Israel and spoke again, saying how beautiful the tents were. He said a star would come out of Jacob and a ruler would rise from Israel. Balak sent him home in anger. Then the book records how Israel was led into unfaithfulness at Peor and suffered a plague. At the end, God told Moses to count the people again, since the old generation had passed away.
d053-stars.why: The blessing stood in spite of what the people did next, which shows that God's promise did not depend on their record.

d054-city_gate.title: The daughters of Zelophehad
d054-city_gate.story: Zelophehad had died with no sons, and his five daughters, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah, came to the door of the tent and asked for a share of their father's land. Moses brought their case to God, who said they were right and that the land should pass to them. Moses was also told to climb the mountain and look at the land, and Joshua was chosen to lead after him.
d054-city_gate.why: The sisters spoke up in public, and the law was changed because they asked.

d055-battle_camp.title: The campaign against Midian
d055-battle_camp.story: Numbers lists the yearly feasts and rules about vows, and then it describes a war against the Midianites, who had led Israel astray at Peor. Twelve thousand men went out, one thousand from each tribe, and they won. The plunder was divided between the soldiers and the rest of the community, and the soldiers brought gold as an offering. The text describes the war as God's judgment, and it is one of the hardest passages in the book to read.
d055-battle_camp.why: It is difficult to read, and honest readers across traditions have wrestled with it.

d056-jordan_ford.title: Settling east of the Jordan
d056-jordan_ford.story: The tribes of Reuben and Gad and half of Manasseh had many animals and asked to settle in the green grazing land east of the Jordan. Moses was angry at first, because he feared they would leave the others to fight alone, as the scouts' fear had once done. They promised to cross over and fight with everyone else before returning, and Moses agreed. Chapter 33 then lists every stop of the journey from Egypt.
d056-jordan_ford.why: The long list of stops is a way of remembering that every camp along the way was part of the story.

d057-hill_town.title: Cities of refuge
d057-hill_town.story: God told Israel to set apart six towns as cities of refuge. A person who killed someone by accident could run to one and be safe from a relative seeking revenge until the community could hear the case. If he was found innocent of murder, he stayed in the town until the high priest died. The people were told that the land was not to be polluted by bloodshed.
d057-hill_town.why: It built a safe place into the law, so that anger could not run ahead of justice.

d058-mountain.title: Leaving Horeb
d058-mountain.story: The book of Numbers closes with the sisters of Zelophehad marrying within their tribe so that the land would stay with their families. Deuteronomy then opens with Moses beginning to speak to Israel on the plains of Moab, near the end of the forty years. He reminds them that God said at Horeb, you have stayed long enough at this mountain, and that he chose leaders to share the work of judging.
d058-mountain.why: Moses begins by looking back, because remembering the road is how a people prepare for what is next.

d059-stone_tablets.title: Keep the commands
d059-stone_tablets.story: Moses told how Israel had beaten the kings Sihon and Og, and how he had asked to cross the Jordan himself but was told he would only see the land from a mountain top. He urged the people to follow God's commands carefully, to not add or take from them, and to teach them to their children. He reminded them that they saw no form at Horeb, only a voice from the fire. He also named cities of refuge east of the Jordan.
d059-stone_tablets.why: Moses was speaking from his own disappointment, and still his main concern was that the people would remember.

d060-house.title: Words on the doorposts
d060-house.story: Moses repeated the Ten Commandments and then gave the words many later people call the Shema: Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. Love him with all your heart, soul and strength. The words were to be taught to children, talked about at home and on the road, bound on the hand and forehead, and written on doorframes and gates. Moses said God chose Israel not because they were big, but because he loved them.
d060-house.why: Faith was meant to be part of ordinary home life, said at the table and on the road, not saved for special days.

d061-covenant_chest.title: New tablets in the ark
d061-covenant_chest.story: Moses told the people to remember how God led them for forty years in the desert and fed them with manna, and not to say that their own strength had made them rich. He also reminded them of the golden calf, the broken tablets, and the second set of tablets that were put in an ark of acacia wood. He asked what God wanted from them: to follow his ways, to love and serve him, and to love the foreigner.
d061-covenant_chest.why: The reminder is that blessing can make people forget, so remembering is a kind of protection.

d062-mountain.title: The mountains of blessing and curse
d062-mountain.story: Moses told Israel to love and obey God and said he was setting before them a blessing and a curse. When they entered the land, they were to put the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal. He said they were to worship at the place God chose, and chapter 13 warns them against false prophets and anyone who would lead them away.
d062-mountain.why: Two mountains stood facing each other, and the choice was set out for everyone to see.

d063-crown.title: Instructions for a king
d063-crown.story: Moses gave rules about clean food, giving a tenth of the harvest, and sharing it with Levites, foreigners, widows and orphans. Every seventh year, debts were to be canceled, and people were to be open-handed with the poor. The people were also told how a future king should act: he was not to collect many horses, wives or silver and gold. He was to copy out the law and read it all his life so that he would not think himself better than others.
d063-crown.why: Even a king was told to read daily and stay humble, long before Israel had one.

d064-city_gate.title: Judges at the gate
d064-city_gate.story: Moses described what share the priests and Levites would receive, and he warned against practices of the nations around them. He said God would raise up a prophet like Moses, and that a message from a prophet could be tested by whether it came true. Judges were to look into cases carefully, elders heard some cases at the town gate, and a person could not be convicted on the word of just one witness. He also set rules for war, and for an unsolved killing.
d064-city_gate.why: Justice was done in the open at the gate, where the whole town could see it.

d065-olive_grove.title: The forgotten sheaf and the olives
d065-olive_grove.story: Moses told the people to return a neighbor's lost ox or donkey, and to build a low wall around a flat roof so no one would fall. A worker's wages were to be paid on the same day, and a poor person's coat taken as a pledge had to be returned by nightfall. If a farmer forgot a sheaf in the field, he was not to go back for it. He was not to beat the olive tree twice or pick the vineyard twice, and what was left belonged to the foreigner, orphan and widow.
d065-olive_grove.why: These small laws look to ordinary things like a forgotten sheaf, and they say generosity should be built into how a person farms.

d066-firstfruits.title: The basket of first fruits
d066-firstfruits.story: When Israel entered the land, each person was to bring a basket of the first harvest and say, my father was a wandering Aramean, and then retell the story of Egypt and the rescue. Everyone, including the Levite and the foreigner, was to celebrate. Moses told them to set up large stones on Mount Ebal, write the law on them, and build an altar. Chapter 28 lists blessings for obedience and warnings for disobedience.
d066-firstfruits.why: The basket was a way of saying thanks and remembering that the harvest was a gift, and the story was told each year.

d067-signpost.title: Choose life
d067-signpost.story: Moses gathered everyone, including children and foreigners, to renew the covenant on the plains of Moab. He said that if they turned away they would be scattered, but if they returned to God with all their heart, God would gather them again. He said the command was not too hard or too far away, but near, in the mouth and heart. Then he said, I have set before you life and death, blessings and curses, so choose life.
d067-signpost.why: It ends on a choice, and it says that the way back is not far off.

d068-scroll.title: Joshua commissioned and the song of Moses
d068-scroll.story: Moses, now 120 years old, told the people that he would not cross the Jordan and that Joshua would lead them. He told Joshua to be strong and courageous, since God would go with him and never leave him. Moses wrote down the law, gave it to the Levites to keep beside the ark, and told them to read it aloud every seventh year. He then taught the people a long song that looks at God as a rock.
d068-scroll.why: Moses handed on both the leadership and the words, and he wrote them down so they would last after he was gone.

d069-mountain.title: A view from Mount Nebo
d069-mountain.story: Moses blessed each of the tribes and then climbed Mount Nebo. God showed him the whole land from there, and said this was the land he had promised to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, though Moses would not enter it. Moses died there in Moab at 120 years old, still strong, and God buried him. The people mourned for thirty days, and Joshua took over as leader.
d069-mountain.why: Moses saw the promise from a distance, and the book says no prophet since had known God face to face as he did.

d070-jericho.title: The walls of Jericho
d070-jericho.story: After crossing into the promised land, Israel came to Jericho, a city shut up tight behind its walls. God gave Joshua unusual instructions: march around the city once a day for six days, with seven priests blowing trumpets in front of the ark of the covenant. On the seventh day they marched around seven times, the priests sounded the trumpets, the people shouted, and the walls fell.
d070-jericho.why: The victory comes through trust and obedience to God's word, not through the strength of the army.

d071-ruins.title: Ai is taken
d071-ruins.story: After Jericho, Israel was defeated at the small town of Ai, because a man named Achan had taken some of the treasure that was set apart for God and hidden it. When Achan was found out and put to death, God told Joshua to try again with an ambush, and this time they took Ai. The people also renewed the covenant on Mount Ebal. Then the nearby Gibeonites tricked Israel into a treaty with old bread and worn sandals, and Israel kept the treaty once the truth came out.
d071-ruins.why: One person's secret hurt a whole community, and a promise made by mistake was still kept.

d072-sun_moon.title: The sun stands still
d072-sun_moon.story: Five kings attacked the town of Gibeon, which had made peace with Israel, and Joshua marched all night to help. God sent large hailstones on the enemy. Joshua asked for the sun to stand still over Gibeon and the moon over the valley, and the text says the sun stopped in the middle of the sky for about a full day. The account says there had been no day like it before or after, because God fought for Israel.
d072-sun_moon.why: Joshua kept his word to an ally, and the writer calls the day unlike any other.

d073-hill_town.title: Caleb asks for Hebron
d073-hill_town.story: Forty-five years after Moses sent him to spy on the land, Caleb came to Joshua and said he was eighty-five and as strong as the day Moses sent him. He asked for the hill country around Hebron, where the large Anakites lived. Joshua blessed him and gave him Hebron, and Caleb drove the Anakites out. His daughter Acsah asked her father for springs of water along with the dry land, and he gave them.
d073-hill_town.why: Caleb had waited most of his life for this promise and still asked for the hard hill, not an easy one.

d074-tabernacle.title: The tent at Shiloh
d074-tabernacle.story: The whole community gathered at Shiloh and set up the tent of meeting there. Seven tribes still had no land, and Joshua asked them how long they would put it off. He sent three men from each tribe to survey the land and write it up in a book. Joshua then cast lots at Shiloh before God to give each tribe its share.
d074-tabernacle.why: The land was divided out by lot in front of the tent, so no one could say it had been given by favor.

d075-city_wall.title: Cities for the Levites
d075-city_wall.story: The last tribes received their lands, and the people gave Joshua a town of his own, Timnath Serah, in the hill country. Six cities of refuge were named for anyone who killed another by accident. The Levites, who had no land, were given forty-eight towns with pasture, spread throughout all the tribes. The writer ends the section by saying that not one of God's good promises had failed.
d075-city_wall.why: People who served in worship were placed in every tribe, so everyone lived near someone who taught the faith.

d076-altar.title: The altar by the Jordan
d076-altar.story: The tribes who lived east of the Jordan returned home with Joshua's blessing, and on the way they built a large altar by the river. When the other tribes heard, they gathered at Shiloh to go to war, but first they sent Phinehas and ten leaders to ask what was going on. The eastern tribes explained that the altar was not for offerings but a witness that they, too, belonged to Israel. Everyone was satisfied, and no fight took place.
d076-altar.why: They asked before they fought, and what looked like betrayal turned out to be a misunderstanding.

d077-oak.title: Joshua's farewell under the oak
d077-oak.story: Joshua, old now, gathered all the tribes at Shechem and told Israel's story from Abraham to the land. He said, if serving the Lord seems undesirable to you, choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve, but as for me and my household, we will serve the Lord. The people said they would too. Joshua set up a large stone under the oak as a witness, and he died at 110.
d077-oak.why: Joshua put the choice plainly before the people and then said clearly what he and his own household would do.

d078-oasis.title: Deborah under the palm
d078-oasis.story: After Joshua, Israel kept drifting from God, and God raised up leaders called judges to rescue them. Othniel, Ehud and Shamgar each brought relief in turn. Then Deborah, a prophet, held court under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel. She told Barak to lead the army against the Canaanite commander Sisera. Barak asked her to go with him, and she did. Israel won, and Deborah and Barak sang a song about it.
d078-oasis.why: Deborah listened for God and spoke with courage, and her steadiness gave Barak the nerve to act.

d079-pitchers.title: Gideon and the three hundred
d079-pitchers.story: When Midian oppressed Israel, Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress, hiding from them, when an angel called him a mighty warrior. Gideon asked for signs and then gathered an army, but God had him send most home until only three hundred were left. At night they surrounded the Midianite camp with trumpets and torches hidden in clay jars. At a signal they broke the jars and blew the trumpets, and the enemy fled.
d079-pitchers.why: Gideon began scared and in hiding, and the victory came with a handful of people and God's help.

d080-watchtower.title: Abimelech and the tower
d080-watchtower.story: Gideon's son Abimelech persuaded the people of Shechem to make him king, and he had most of his brothers killed to secure it. One brother, Jotham, escaped and told a story about trees that ended up asking a thornbush to be their king. After a few years Abimelech's rule fell apart. At the tower of Thebez, a woman dropped a millstone on him, and the account says this was how God paid him back. Two more judges followed, Tola and Jair.
d080-watchtower.why: It is a dark story about a man who grabbed power, and it ends with him falling to a millstone.

d081-altar.title: Samson's birth announced
d081-altar.story: Jephthah, a leader from Gilead, made a rash vow before going into battle, and the account tells without softening how it cost him his daughter. Then Israel again did wrong and the Philistines ruled them for forty years. An angel appeared to a childless woman, the wife of Manoah, and told her she would have a son who was to be set apart for God from birth and would begin to rescue Israel. The boy, Samson, was born and grew, and God blessed him.
d081-altar.why: The first story is painful, and the second one starts with hope, which is how this book moves from one to the other.

d082-samson_pillars.title: Samson at Gaza
d082-samson_pillars.story: Samson was very strong, and the book shows him making rash choices. At his wedding feast he told a riddle, and when it was betrayed he struck out at the Philistines. He tied torches to foxes and set their fields on fire, and he once struck down many men with a donkey's jawbone. In Gaza he carried the city gate to the top of a hill. Later Delilah learned the secret of his hair, and he was captured and blinded. At a festival in the temple of Dagon, he prayed, pushed the pillars apart, and the building fell, with him in it.
d082-samson_pillars.why: Samson was gifted and flawed, and the book is honest that God worked through a person who was far from perfect.

d083-battle_camp.title: The tribes gather at Gibeah
d083-battle_camp.story: Near the end of Judges the book says there was no king in Israel and everyone did as they saw fit. A Levite and his concubine stopped for the night in Gibeah, in the land of Benjamin, where the men of the town abused her and she died. The Levite sent word to all the tribes, and Israel gathered and demanded that Benjamin hand over the men responsible. Benjamin refused, and a civil war followed that nearly wiped out the tribe.
d083-battle_camp.why: It is one of the darkest chapters in the Bible, and it is told to show how bad things get when people do whatever seems right to them.

d084-harvest.title: Ruth gleans in the barley
d084-harvest.story: After her husband died, Ruth stayed with her mother-in-law Naomi and traveled with her from Moab to Bethlehem. It was the barley harvest, and Ruth went out to glean, gathering the grain the reapers left behind, in the field of a man named Boaz. Boaz had heard of her loyalty to Naomi and made sure she had enough to eat and was safe. The book ends with Boaz marrying Ruth, and the family line that follows leads to King David.
d084-harvest.why: It is a quiet story of loyalty and kindness, showing God's care at work through ordinary harvests and families.

d085-city_gate.title: Boaz at the gate
d085-city_gate.story: Naomi told Ruth to go to Boaz at the threshing floor at night and ask him to act as a family protector. Boaz praised her faithfulness and promised to do it. The next morning he went to the town gate and met with ten elders and a closer relative, who then gave up his claim. Boaz bought the family land and took Ruth as his wife. They had a son, Obed, who was the grandfather of David.
d085-city_gate.why: Ruth was a foreigner and a widow, and she became part of the family line that led to a king.

d086-covenant_chest.title: The ark is captured
d086-covenant_chest.story: As a boy, Samuel slept in the house of God at Shiloh, and one night he heard his name called three times, thinking it was Eli. Eli told him to say, speak, Lord, your servant is listening. Later Israel carried the ark into battle against the Philistines and lost. The ark was captured, Eli's sons were killed, and Eli died when he heard. In the temple of Dagon, the Philistines found the idol fallen on its face before the ark.
d086-covenant_chest.why: Samuel's willingness to listen was the start of his ministry, and Israel learned that the ark could not be used as a lucky charm.

d087-cairn.title: Ebenezer, the stone of help
d087-cairn.story: The Philistines suffered under plagues while they held the ark, so they put it on a new cart pulled by two cows with gold gifts, and the cows went straight back toward Israel. After twenty years, Samuel called the people to return to God, and at Mizpah the Philistines were driven back. Samuel set up a stone and named it Ebenezer, which means stone of help, saying, thus far the Lord has helped us.
d087-cairn.why: The stone was a marker of gratitude, and it looked back over the road and said thanks.

d088-oil_jars.title: Saul is anointed
d088-oil_jars.story: Samuel took a flask of oil and poured it on the head of Saul, the tall young man who had come looking for his father's lost donkeys, and told him the Lord had chosen him to lead Israel. At Mizpah, when Saul was named, he was found hiding among the baggage. Later Saul grew impatient and offered a sacrifice himself, and Samuel said his kingdom would not last.
d088-oil_jars.why: The first king was chosen by the people's wish, and the story is open about both his promise and his weakness.

d089-mountain.title: Jonathan's climb at Michmash
d089-mountain.story: Jonathan, Saul's son, and his armor-bearer climbed a steep cliff to a Philistine outpost, saying, perhaps the Lord will act for us. They killed about twenty men, and panic spread through the whole Philistine army. Later God sent Saul to destroy the Amalekites, but Saul spared their king and the best animals. Samuel told him that to obey is better than sacrifice, and that God had rejected him as king.
d089-mountain.why: Jonathan trusted God with a small risk and Saul missed the point of obeying, and the two stories sit side by side.

d090-stones.title: David and Goliath
d090-stones.story: Israel's army faced the Philistines across a valley, and for forty days a giant named Goliath challenged anyone to fight him. No one dared, until David, a young shepherd who had come to bring food to his brothers, stepped forward. Saul offered him armor, but David took his staff, his sling and five smooth stones from the stream instead. He told Goliath he came in the name of the Lord, and one stone from his sling brought the giant down.
d090-stones.why: The story is told as a victory that depends on God, not on size or weapons.

d091-harp.title: David's harp and Jonathan's friendship
d091-harp.story: David played the harp for Saul to calm him, but Saul grew jealous when the women sang that David had killed tens of thousands. Twice Saul threw a spear at him. Jonathan, Saul's son, loved David as himself, and they made a covenant of friendship. Jonathan spoke up for David and then warned him by shooting arrows as a signal. They parted in tears, and David went into hiding.
d091-harp.why: Jonathan chose loyalty to a friend over his own claim to the throne, and that is a rare and costly kind of love.

d092-cave.title: The cave of Adullam
d092-cave.story: David fled to the priest at Nob, who gave him the holy bread and Goliath's sword, and then to the cave of Adullam. His brothers and his father's household joined him there, along with about four hundred men who were in distress, in debt or discontented. Saul had the priests of Nob killed, and one of them, Abiathar, escaped to David. Saul chased David through the wilderness, and Jonathan came to encourage him.
d092-cave.why: David's first followers were people who had nowhere else to go, and they became a band that stuck together.

d093-tent_camp.title: The spear and the water jug
d093-tent_camp.story: David was hiding from King Saul, who was hunting him with three thousand soldiers. Twice David had Saul at his mercy, once in a cave and once in the camp while Saul slept, and each time he refused to harm the Lord's anointed. In the camp he took only Saul's spear and water jug and called to Saul from a distance to show he meant no harm. Between these scenes, Abigail met David on the road with food and talked him out of taking revenge on her husband Nabal.
d093-tent_camp.why: Mercy is hardest when you have the power to strike back, and these chapters show restraint as a kind of strength.

d094-ruins.title: Ziklag burned and recovered
d094-ruins.story: David and his men came home to Ziklag and found the town burned and their families taken. His own men talked of stoning him, but David found strength in the Lord, followed the raiders and brought everyone back safe. Before that, Saul was afraid of the Philistine army and went at night to a medium at Endor, and he heard only bad news about the coming battle. The two stories sit side by side: one man who found strength in God in distress, and one who turned to a medium when the Lord no longer answered him.
d094-ruins.why: Loss and fear are real, and the story asks where we turn when everything has been taken.

d095-mountain.title: Saul falls on Gilboa
d095-mountain.story: The Philistines fought Israel on Mount Gilboa, and Saul and his sons, including Jonathan, were killed. When David heard, he tore his clothes and took up a lament, saying how the mighty had fallen, and he grieved for Jonathan as a dear friend. Afterward David went up to Hebron, and the men of Judah made him king over their tribe. A long struggle with Saul's house followed, and Abner, Saul's general, finally turned toward David before he was killed.
d095-mountain.why: David mourned the king who had hunted him, which shows that grief and honesty can sit together.

d096-covenant_chest.title: The ark comes to Jerusalem
d096-covenant_chest.story: David became king over all Israel and took the hilltop city of Jerusalem, which became his capital. He wanted the ark of God brought there. The first attempt ended badly when Uzzah touched the ark and died, and David stopped to rethink. Three months later the ark was carried in properly, with shouting and trumpets, and David danced before the Lord with all his strength.
d096-covenant_chest.why: Joy in worship can be loud and wholehearted, and care matters as much as enthusiasm.

d097-palace.title: The promise of an enduring house
d097-palace.story: David wanted to build a house for God, but through the prophet Nathan the Lord said he would build David a house instead, a line of kings that would last. David sat before the Lord in thanks and wonder. Later he gave Jonathan's son Mephibosheth, who was lame in both feet, a place at the king's table. Then the story turns: David took Bathsheba, another man's wife, and arranged for her husband Uriah to be killed in battle.
d097-palace.why: The same chapters hold great promise and great failure, and the Bible does not hide the failures of even its great kings.

d098-lamb.title: Nathan's story of the little lamb
d098-lamb.story: The Lord sent Nathan to David with a story about a rich man with many flocks who took the one small lamb of a poor man, a lamb that was like a daughter to him. David was angry and said the rich man must pay. Nathan answered, "You are that man!" and named what David had done to Uriah. David said, "I have sinned against the Lord," and Nathan told him he would not die, though hard consequences would follow in his family.
d098-lamb.why: Telling the truth about our wrongs is painful, and the story shows honesty leading toward forgiveness.

d099-city_gate.title: Absalom steals hearts at the gate
d099-city_gate.story: Absalom, David's son, was brought back to Jerusalem after living away in exile. He began rising early to stand by the city gate, greeting people with a warm word and promising that he would judge their cases fairly. In this way, the text says, he stole the hearts of the men of Israel. After some years he declared himself king at Hebron, and David left Jerusalem in tears with his household and loyal men.
d099-city_gate.why: Charm and flattery can win a crowd, but the story invites us to look at who really cares for people.

d100-oak.title: Absalom caught in the oak
d100-oak.story: The battle between David's army and Absalom's men was fought in the forest of Ephraim. David asked the commanders to deal gently with Absalom for his sake. As Absalom rode a mule, his head was caught in the branches of a great oak, and he was left hanging. Joab and his armor bearers killed him, and when the news came David wept, crying, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom!" Joab told him the army needed to see him, and David went and sat in the gate.
d100-oak.why: Even a king grieved like any parent, and the chapter does not hurry past sorrow.

d101-harp.title: David's song of praise
d101-harp.story: After a revolt is put down and a famine passes, these chapters give the long song David sang to the Lord on the day he was rescued from his enemies and from Saul. He called God his rock, his fortress and his deliverer. He remembered being surrounded and crying out for help, and he said God heard from his temple and brought him out into a broad place. The song gives credit to God for his rescue and for the strength he had.
d101-harp.why: The song shows gratitude spoken aloud, remembering help that came when it felt out of reach.

d102-well.title: Water from the well at Bethlehem
d102-well.story: David was in a stronghold while the Philistines held Bethlehem, and he said how much he longed for a drink from the well by the gate of his hometown. Three of his mighty men broke through the enemy camp, drew the water and carried it back to him. David would not drink it. He poured it out before the Lord and said it was too costly, because it was like the blood of men who risked their lives.
d102-well.why: The story honors loyalty and shows a leader treating a gift of sacrifice as something sacred.

d103-oil_jars.title: Solomon anointed king
d103-oil_jars.story: When David was old, his son Adonijah began to set himself up as the next king. Nathan the prophet and Bathsheba went to David, and he promised that Solomon would be king after him. Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tent and anointed Solomon, the ram's horn was blown, and all the people shouted for the new king. In chapter 2 David told Solomon to be strong and to follow the ways of the Lord, and then David died.
d103-oil_jars.why: Power passed from one king to the next with a charge to follow God's ways, which is the measure the writers use for every king after.

d104-crown.title: Solomon's wise heart
d104-crown.story: Solomon, now king, loved the Lord and made an offering at Gibeon. That night God asked what he should give him, and Solomon asked for an understanding heart to govern the people well. God was pleased and promised wisdom along with riches and honor. Soon after, two women came to Solomon with one baby they both claimed, and his wise ruling revealed which was the true mother. The chapters then describe his officials, his peaceful kingdom and his famous wisdom.
d104-crown.why: Solomon asked for wisdom before wealth, and the story invites us to notice what we ask for first.

d105-cedar.title: Cedar for the temple
d105-cedar.story: Solomon made an agreement with King Hiram of Tyre, who sent cedar and other timber from Lebanon in exchange for food. Thousands of workers cut and carried stone and wood, and the temple stones were shaped at the quarry so no hammer was heard on site. Work began in the fourth year of Solomon's reign and took seven years. The text gives the measures of the rooms, the carved cherubim and the gold, and it also mentions the palace Solomon built for himself over thirteen years.
d105-cedar.why: A great work takes years of shared labor, and these chapters celebrate that patience.

d106-temple.title: The temple dedicated
d106-temple.story: After David, his son Solomon became king and, in the fourth year of his reign, began to build the temple in Jerusalem. The work took seven years and used cedar, stone and gold. When it was finished, the priests brought the ark of the covenant into it, and a cloud filled the house. Solomon stood before the people and prayed, asking God to hear whenever they prayed toward this place.
d106-temple.why: The temple was the center of Israel's worship, and Solomon's prayer shows the hope of a place where people meet God and are heard.

d106-covenant_chest.title: The temple dedicated
d106-covenant_chest.story: After David, his son Solomon became king and, in the fourth year of his reign, began to build the temple in Jerusalem. The work took seven years and used cedar, stone and gold. When it was finished, the priests brought the ark of the covenant into it, and a cloud filled the house. Solomon stood before the people and prayed, asking God to hear whenever they prayed toward this place.
d106-covenant_chest.why: The temple was the center of Israel's worship, and Solomon's prayer shows the hope of a place where people meet God and are heard.

d107-caravan.title: The queen of Sheba visits
d107-caravan.story: The queen of Sheba heard of Solomon's fame and traveled to Jerusalem with a caravan of camels carrying spices, gold and jewels. She tested him with hard questions, and he answered all of them. She saw his house, his food and his servants, and said that what she had heard had not told the half. Later chapters turn sadder, as Solomon married many foreign wives and his heart was drawn away from the Lord, and the text says the kingdom would be divided afterward.
d107-caravan.why: The visit shows wisdom drawing admiration, and the ending warns that a good start is not a guarantee.

d108-golden_calf.title: The golden calves at Bethel and Dan
d108-golden_calf.story: After Solomon died, his son Rehoboam rejected the older advisers and told the people he would make their burden heavier. Ten tribes broke away under Jeroboam, and only Judah and Benjamin stayed with Rehoboam. Jeroboam feared that his people would drift back if they went to the temple in Jerusalem, so he set up two golden calves, one at Bethel and one at Dan. A prophet from Judah came to speak against the altar at Bethel, but even after that, Jeroboam did not turn from his ways.
d108-golden_calf.why: The story shows how fear for power can lead people to build their own religion in place of trust.

d109-altar.title: Ahab and Jezebel turn to Baal
d109-altar.story: After Solomon's kingdom split in two, one king after another in the north and the south did what was evil in the eyes of the Lord. Ahab son of Omri became king of Israel in Samaria and did more evil than any king before him. He married Jezebel, the daughter of a Sidonian king, and began to serve Baal and worship him. He built an altar for Baal in a temple of Baal in Samaria and made an Asherah pole, so that one king's choices pulled the whole nation toward another god.
d109-altar.why: One household's choices can pull a whole nation off course, and this sets the stage for Elijah's challenge to the people in the next chapters.

d110-carmel.title: The contest on Carmel
d110-carmel.story: Under King Ahab and Queen Jezebel, many in Israel had turned to the god Baal. The prophet Elijah called the people to Mount Carmel and set a challenge: each side would prepare a sacrifice and call on their god to send fire. The prophets of Baal called from morning until evening and nothing happened. Elijah had water poured over his sacrifice and altar three times, offered a short prayer, and fire fell and burned up everything. The people fell down and said that the Lord is God.
d110-carmel.why: The scene asks the people to choose whom they will trust, and it is still a story about divided loyalties.

d110-stream.title: The contest on Carmel
d110-stream.story: Under King Ahab and Queen Jezebel, many in Israel had turned to the god Baal. The prophet Elijah called the people to Mount Carmel and set a challenge: each side would prepare a sacrifice and call on their god to send fire. The prophets of Baal called from morning until evening and nothing happened. Elijah had water poured over his sacrifice and altar three times, offered a short prayer, and fire fell and burned up everything. The people fell down and said that the Lord is God.
d110-stream.why: The scene asks the people to choose whom they will trust, and it is still a story about divided loyalties.

d111-cave.title: The quiet voice at Horeb
d111-cave.story: Fearing Queen Jezebel's threat, Elijah ran into the wilderness, sat under a broom bush and asked to die. An angel gave him food and water twice, and he walked forty days to Horeb, the mountain of God. There a great wind, an earthquake and a fire passed by, but the Lord was not in any of them. Then came a still, small voice, and Elijah went out to the mouth of the cave, where God spoke to him and gave him work to do and told him that seven thousand in Israel had not bowed to Baal.
d111-cave.why: God met a worn out prophet gently, with food and rest first and words after.

d112-battle_camp.title: Micaiah and Ahab's last battle
d112-battle_camp.story: King Ahab of Israel asked King Jehoshaphat of Judah to help him take Ramoth Gilead from Aram. About four hundred prophets promised victory, but Jehoshaphat asked for a prophet of the Lord, and Micaiah said he saw Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd. Ahab had him put in prison and went into battle in disguise. An arrow shot without special aim struck him between the joints of his armor, and he died that evening. In 2 Kings 1 his son Ahaziah was hurt in a fall, and Elijah told him he would die.
d112-battle_camp.why: Telling an unwelcome truth costs something, and the story respects the person who did it anyway.

d113-whirlwind.title: Elijah taken up in a whirlwind
d113-whirlwind.story: Elijah and Elisha walked together, and Elisha refused to leave his master's side. At the Jordan Elijah struck the water with his cloak and they crossed on dry ground. Then a chariot and horses of fire separated them, and Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind. Elisha picked up the fallen cloak, struck the river, and the water parted for him too. The rest of the chapters tell of his early work, including the widow's oil and a child restored.
d113-whirlwind.why: The story is about one generation handing its work to the next, and the next one picking it up.

d114-jordan_ford.title: Naaman dips in the Jordan
d114-jordan_ford.story: Naaman, commander of the Aramean army, had a skin disease, and a young Israelite girl who served his wife told her about a prophet in Samaria. Elisha sent a messenger telling him to wash seven times in the Jordan. Naaman was angry at the plain instructions and nearly went home, but his servants urged him to try. He washed, and his skin became like a child's. He declared that there was no God in all the earth but Israel's. The next chapters include the siege of Samaria, ending with food at the gate.
d114-jordan_ford.why: It was a servant girl and Naaman's own servants who pointed him toward healing, which shows help can come from ordinary people.

d115-chariot.title: Jehu drives to Jezreel
d115-chariot.story: Elisha sent a young prophet to anoint Jehu, a commander, as king over Israel and to end Ahab's house. Jehu drove his chariot furiously to Jezreel, and the watchman said he drove like a madman. He killed King Joram and other rulers, and Jezebel was thrown from a window. The story is violent and the text presents it as the end of Ahab's family. Chapter 10 follows Jehu as he wipes out the rest of Ahab's family and the worshipers of Baal.
d115-chariot.why: This passage is hard reading, and it shows that wrongdoing in power has real consequences.

d116-crown.title: The hidden prince crowned
d116-crown.story: After Ahaziah died, Athaliah seized the throne of Judah and tried to kill the royal family. Jehosheba hid the baby Joash, and for six years he lived in the temple. In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada gathered the guards, crowned Joash and showed him to the people. They shouted, "Long live the king!" Joash later ordered repairs to the temple, with money collected in a chest. Chapter 13 tells of Elisha's death.
d116-crown.why: One woman's quiet courage kept a child alive, and with him the line of David's kings.

d117-altar.title: Ahaz copies a foreign altar
d117-altar.story: Ahaz became king of Judah and followed the practices of other nations, even sacrificing his son in the fire. When Aram and Israel attacked him, he took silver and gold from the temple and sent it to the king of Assyria to buy help. In Damascus he saw an altar he liked and sent the design to the priest Uriah, who built a copy in Jerusalem. Ahaz moved the temple's bronze altar aside and used the new one. Chapters 14 and 15 move quickly through other kings of Judah and Israel in the same period.
d117-altar.why: Copying what looks powerful around us can slowly crowd out what we were meant to keep.

d118-serpent_pole.title: Hezekiah breaks the serpent
d118-serpent_pole.story: Assyria conquered the northern kingdom of Israel and carried many of its people away, and the text explains this as the result of ignoring God's warnings. In Judah, Hezekiah did what was right. He removed the shrines, smashed the sacred stones, and broke the bronze serpent Moses had made, because people had been burning incense to it. Then Sennacherib of Assyria came against Judah's cities, and his officer shouted taunts at the wall in Hebrew.
d118-serpent_pole.why: Even something once given for good can become an idol, and Hezekiah was willing to break it.

d119-sundial.title: Hezekiah's shadow goes back
d119-sundial.story: Hezekiah received a threatening letter from Sennacherib, took it to the temple, spread it before the Lord and prayed. Isaiah told him God had heard, and the Assyrian army left. In those days Hezekiah became deathly ill, and he prayed again and was given fifteen more years. As a sign, the shadow on the stairway went back ten steps. The next chapters tell of his son Manasseh, who ruled long and did great wrong, and then of Amon.
d119-sundial.why: The story shows a king taking his fear to God in prayer, and God answering twice.

d120-scroll.title: The book of the law found
d120-scroll.story: Josiah became king at eight and started repairing the temple when he was grown. While the workers were at it, the high priest Hilkiah found the book of the law. When it was read to Josiah he tore his clothes, and the prophet Huldah said judgment would still come but not in his lifetime. Josiah gathered the people and renewed the covenant, removed idols and kept the Passover. The book ends with Babylon taking Jerusalem and the temple burned, and a glimmer of mercy for the exiled king Jehoiachin.
d120-scroll.why: Finding the old words again moved a king to change, and the book still asks that of readers.

d121-oak.title: The family tree
d121-oak.story: First Chronicles opens with names. It begins with Adam and moves through Noah's sons, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and then the twelve tribes of Israel. It lists Esau's line and the kings of Edom, and then follows Judah and the family of David in detail. The list is long and sounds like a family record read aloud.
d121-oak.why: The long list says that every person in this story was remembered by name, and none was forgotten.

d122-hill_town.title: Judah's clans and Jabez
d122-hill_town.story: Chronicles continues with the family of David, listing his sons born in Hebron and Jerusalem and the line of kings that followed him. It then turns to the clans of Judah and other families. In the middle is a short story about Jabez, who was born in pain and prayed that God would bless him and keep him from harm. The text says God granted what he asked.
d122-hill_town.why: A short prayer in a long list of names reminds us that each person is counted and heard.

d123-tent_camp.title: The tribes and the Levites
d123-tent_camp.story: First Chronicles records the tribes of Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh in the east and notes that they went into exile for unfaithfulness. It then lists the line of Levi, including the priests, Aaron's family and the clans who served in the tent and temple. It names the Levites assigned to music and care of the tent, and the towns where they lived.
