d123-tent_camp.why: Those who served in the background were written down too, and their work counted.

d124-signpost.title: The other tribes listed
d124-signpost.story: This chapter keeps listing the tribes, Issachar, Benjamin, Naphtali, Manasseh, Ephraim and Asher, along with their clans and fighting men. The lists give numbers of warriors and family heads and mention a few events, such as a raid on cattle and the sorrow of Ephraim. Each family has a place in the record, with the people named together.
d124-signpost.why: In a record like this, belonging to a family and a people matters more than any single story.

d125-scroll.title: The registry of those who returned
d125-scroll.story: After more lists of Benjamin's family, the writer gives a registry of those who lived in Jerusalem after the exile. It names families, priests, Levites, gatekeepers and the people who looked after the temple, and it notes who sang day and night. These were the first to settle again in their towns after the return. The passage also repeats the line of King Saul.
d125-scroll.why: A rebuilt community starts with ordinary people taking their places again, one family and one name at a time.

d126-crown.title: David made king
d126-crown.story: Chronicles tells Saul's death briefly, then gets to David. All Israel came to him at Hebron and said, "We are your own flesh and blood," and they anointed him king. David took Jerusalem, and his mighty men are named and honored. Soldiers from every tribe came to join him, ready to help, and the passage says they were of one mind to make David king.
d126-crown.why: The story is about people from many backgrounds choosing to stand together behind one leader and one purpose.

d127-covenant_chest.title: The ark carried with songs
d127-covenant_chest.story: David gathered the leaders and went to bring the ark to Jerusalem. After a first failed attempt, he prepared a tent for it and had the Levites carry it as the law said. David and the people played harps, lyres, cymbals and trumpets, and David danced. He then gave a psalm of thanks, calling everyone to sing to the Lord, make his deeds known and give thanks for his steady love.
d127-covenant_chest.why: The song shows thankfulness turned into music that anyone in the whole crowd can join in singing.

d128-palace.title: The promise to David
d128-palace.story: David noticed he was living in a house of cedar while the ark sat in a tent, and he wanted to build God a house. Through Nathan, God told him that David would not build it, but that his son would, and that God would establish David's house for good. David sat before the Lord and prayed with amazement that God had brought him this far. Chapter 18 summarizes David's victories and the officials who served him.
d128-palace.why: The promise came before anything was built, which makes it a gift given ahead of any work.

d129-altar.title: The threshing floor and the plans
d129-altar.story: After wars with Ammon and Aram, David made a census of Israel, which displeased God, and a plague struck the people. When David saw the angel by the threshing floor of Ornan, he asked to buy it, saying he would not give God what cost him nothing. He built an altar there, and the plague stopped. David then gathered stone, iron, bronze and cedar for the temple and told Solomon he would be the builder. He also organized the Levites for their work.
d129-altar.why: David insisted on paying a real price, and the story links honesty about failure with generous giving.

d130-harp.title: Musicians appointed
d130-harp.story: David and the leaders set apart men from the families of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun for the work of music. They played lyres, harps and cymbals in the house of the Lord, and some prophesied with music. There were two hundred and eighty-eight of them, all trained and skilled, and they were assigned by lot, young and old alike. Before this the priests were also organized into twenty-four divisions.
d130-harp.why: Music was treated as real service to God, with trained people giving their craft day and night.

d131-scroll.title: David gives Solomon the plans
d131-scroll.story: David organized the gatekeepers, treasurers, officials and army commanders. Then he gathered the leaders and told them he had wanted to build a house for God but God had said no, because he was a man of war. God had chosen Solomon instead, and David gave him the plans for the temple, its rooms, its furnishings and the work of the priests, saying they came from the Lord's hand. He told his son to be strong and do the work.
d131-scroll.why: David passed on the work along with plans and encouragement, trusting someone else to finish what he began.

d132-temple.title: Building on Mount Moriah
d132-temple.story: David praised God before the whole assembly and prayed, "Everything comes from you, and from your own hand we have given to you." The people gave gifts with willing hearts, and Solomon was acknowledged as king. In 2 Chronicles, Solomon went to Gibeon and asked God for wisdom to lead the people, and God gave him that, along with wealth. He then began to build the temple on Mount Moriah, with the help of workers and timber from Tyre.
d132-temple.why: Giving is shown as something that begins with gratitude, since everything already came from God.

d133-covenant_chest.title: The ark inside and fire falls
d133-covenant_chest.story: When the temple was finished, the priests brought the ark into the inner room. The singers and musicians gave thanks together, and a cloud filled the house so the priests could not continue. Solomon prayed, asking God to hear his people when they prayed toward the temple. When he finished, fire came down from heaven on the offerings and the glory of the Lord filled the house. The people bowed with their faces to the ground. Later the Lord appeared to Solomon, with a promise and a warning.
d133-covenant_chest.why: The scene is about God arriving in a place made ready, and the people responding with praise.

d134-city_wall.title: Rehoboam strengthens the cities
d134-city_wall.story: Chronicles briefly records Solomon's building, his ships to Ophir and the visit of the queen of Sheba. After Solomon died, his son Rehoboam would not listen to the older advisers, and the northern tribes broke away. When he gathered an army to win them back, the prophet Shemaiah told him not to fight his brothers, and he listened. He built fortified cities in Judah, and priests and Levites from the north came to stand with him. For three years they walked in the way of David and Solomon, and the kingdom grew strong.
d134-city_wall.why: Strong walls help, but the passage suggests that listening to wise voices matters even more than defenses.

d135-shofar.title: Asa renews the covenant
d135-shofar.story: King Shishak of Egypt attacked Judah, and the prophet Shemaiah told Rehoboam that the Lord had left them because they had left him. The leaders humbled themselves and the disaster was lessened. Later, King Asa removed foreign altars and idols, and he called the people to a covenant. They made an oath with shouting, trumpets and horns and sought God with their whole heart, and the Lord gave them rest.
d135-shofar.why: A fresh start can be a shared decision, with a community choosing together to turn back.

d136-battle_camp.title: Singers go before the army
d136-battle_camp.story: A great army from Moab and Ammon came against Judah, and King Jehoshaphat was afraid. He called a fast and prayed in front of the people, saying, "We do not know what to do, but our eyes are upon you." A Levite named Jahaziel told them not to fear because the battle was God's. The next morning Jehoshaphat sent singers ahead of the army to praise the Lord, and the enemies turned on each other. Judah only had to collect the spoil.
d136-battle_camp.why: Not knowing what to do is a fine place to pray from, and the story shows singing before any victory.

d137-palace.title: Athaliah and the hidden king
d137-palace.story: Jehoram ruled Judah and did evil, and his son Ahaziah reigned a year before he was killed. Then Athaliah, Ahaziah's mother, destroyed the royal family and seized power. Jehoshabeath, Ahaziah's sister, hid the infant Joash in the temple. In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada gathered the commanders and crowned him with a covenant before the Lord. Athaliah was put to death, the people rejoiced and the city was quiet.
d137-palace.why: A hidden child and a few brave adults changed a nation's future by acting quietly at the right time.

d138-treasury.title: Joash repairs the temple
d138-treasury.story: Joash did right while the priest Jehoiada lived and decided to repair the temple. He asked the Levites to collect money, and when they were slow, he had a chest set by the gate of the temple. The people brought gifts gladly and the chest was emptied and refilled many times, so the builders were able to restore the house. After Jehoiada died Joash drifted away. The next chapters cover Amaziah, Uzziah and Jotham, some good and some flawed.
d138-treasury.why: The chest at the door shows a community giving together, one coin at a time.

d139-lampstand.title: The temple cleansed
d139-lampstand.story: Ahaz shut the temple doors and set up altars everywhere, but his son Hezekiah opened the doors in the first month of his reign. He told the priests and Levites to cleanse the house and take out everything unclean, which took sixteen days. The people then offered sacrifices with music. Hezekiah sent word across the land inviting everyone, even from the north, to come to Jerusalem for the Passover, and the people kept the feast for fourteen days with great joy.
d139-lampstand.why: Opening the doors again is the picture here, a welcome offered to anyone willing to return.

d140-city_wall.title: Hezekiah's defense
d140-city_wall.story: After the Passover, the people destroyed idols across the land, and Hezekiah organized the priests and gave generously to support them. When Sennacherib of Assyria invaded Judah, Hezekiah blocked the springs outside the city, repaired the wall and built another one. He told the people to be strong because there was greater power with them than with the Assyrians. He and Isaiah prayed, and the Lord sent an angel who turned the Assyrians back. Chapter 33 turns to Manasseh and his later repentance.
d140-city_wall.why: Hezekiah prepared hard and prayed hard, and the text sees no conflict between the two.

d141-scroll.title: The law found and the decree of Cyrus
d141-scroll.story: Josiah became king as a boy and, as he grew, rid the land of idols and repaired the temple. The priest Hilkiah found the book of the law, and when it was read to him, Josiah wept and sought the Lord. He kept a great Passover. The book then moves through the last kings of Judah, ending with the fall of Jerusalem and the exile to Babylon. In the final verses Cyrus of Persia declares that the people may go home and build the temple.
d141-scroll.why: The last words of Chronicles are an invitation to go home, so the book ends on hope.

d142-altar.title: The altar rebuilt
d142-altar.story: Cyrus, king of Persia, announced that God had told him to build a temple in Jerusalem and that any of God's people could go. More than forty thousand returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, carrying the temple vessels that had been taken away. When they arrived, they first set up the altar on its old site and began offering sacrifices, even though they were afraid of the people around them. In the second year they laid the temple foundation, and the people shouted for joy while the older ones, who remembered the first house, wept aloud.
d142-altar.why: The first thing rebuilt was the place to meet God, and the sound of that day mixed joy and grief.

d143-temple.title: The temple finished
d143-temple.story: Neighbors who opposed the Jews tried to stop the building with letters to the Persian kings, and the work halted for years. Then the prophets Haggai and Zechariah encouraged the people, and Zerubbabel and Jeshua started again. King Darius found Cyrus's decree and allowed the work to go on, and the temple was finished and dedicated with joy. Later Ezra, a priest and scribe who knew the law well, traveled from Babylon to Jerusalem with the king's blessing to teach the people.
d143-temple.why: The work stalled and then restarted, which says that unfinished work can still be picked back up.

d144-caravan.title: Ezra's company and the river fast
d144-caravan.story: Ezra gathered a company of families and priests at the river Ahava before they left Babylon. He was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers to guard them, since he had said God protects those who seek him, so they fasted and prayed for safe travel instead. They arrived safely in Jerusalem. Then leaders told Ezra many had married people from other nations and taken up their customs, and he tore his clothes and sat appalled. The people wept and agreed to make a change.
d144-caravan.why: The fast by the river shows travelers placing their safety in God's hands, with prayer as their guard.

d145-city_wall.title: Nehemiah and the broken wall
d145-city_wall.story: Nehemiah served as cupbearer to the Persian king. When his brother told him that the wall of Jerusalem was broken down and its gates burned, he sat down and wept, fasted and prayed for days. When the king asked why he looked sad, Nehemiah prayed quickly and then asked to go and rebuild. The king agreed and gave him letters. Nehemiah rode out at night to inspect the ruined wall, then told the leaders, "Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem," and families took sections to repair.
d145-city_wall.why: Nehemiah prayed first and then acted, and the work was shared among ordinary families, each one building a section.

d146-watchtower.title: Builders armed and working
d146-watchtower.story: Sanballat and Tobiah mocked the builders and plotted against them. Nehemiah prayed and posted guards, and from then on half the men worked while half held spears. Those carrying loads held a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other, and a trumpeter stood by to sound a warning. Nehemiah also dealt with a complaint that the poor were being squeezed by debt. The wall was finished in fifty-two days, and the enemies lost their confidence.
d146-watchtower.why: Work and watchfulness went together, and justice for the poor was part of the job.

d147-city_gate.title: The law read at the Water Gate
d147-city_gate.story: The people gathered in the square by the Water Gate and asked Ezra to bring out the book of the law. He read from early morning until midday while the Levites explained the meaning, and the people stood and listened. They wept when they heard it, but Nehemiah and Ezra told them not to grieve, because the joy of the Lord was their strength. They kept the feast of booths and then gathered to confess and recall God's story with a long prayer.
d147-city_gate.why: Hearing the words again brought tears first and then joy, and the leaders let both be real.

d148-hill_town.title: The people settle Jerusalem
d148-hill_town.story: The leaders, Levites and priests sealed a written covenant promising to follow God's law, keep the Sabbath and support the temple. They drew lots so that one in every ten families would move into Jerusalem, since the city had few residents, and the rest stayed in their towns. Some volunteered, and the people blessed them. The chapters list the families and where they lived.
d148-hill_town.why: A city needs people willing to live in it, and the story honors those who moved in.

d149-shofar.title: The wall dedicated
d149-shofar.story: The wall was dedicated with a great celebration. Levites were brought from all around to sing thanksgiving songs with cymbals, harps and lyres, and Nehemiah set two large thanksgiving choirs walking in opposite directions along the top of the wall, with Ezra leading one and Nehemiah following the other. They met at the temple and offered sacrifices, and the sound of the rejoicing was heard far away. In chapter 13 Nehemiah returned after a time away and found some practices he had to correct.
d149-shofar.why: The wall was not only for defense, it became a place to walk and sing together.

d150-palace.title: Esther becomes queen
d150-palace.story: King Xerxes held a great feast and Queen Vashti refused to come when he called her, so she was removed. A search began for a new queen, and a young Jewish woman named Esther, raised by her cousin Mordecai, was chosen, and she did not tell anyone her background. Haman, the king's chief official, became angry when Mordecai would not bow to him, and he persuaded the king to order the destruction of all Jews. Mordecai urged Esther to speak, saying maybe she had come to her position for such a time as this, and she asked the Jews to fast for three days.
d150-palace.why: Esther took a risk because the moment called for it, and she did not go alone.

d151-crown.title: Mordecai honored
d151-crown.story: One night the king could not sleep and had the royal records read to him, and he learned that Mordecai had once saved his life without reward. Haman, thinking the honor was for himself, ended up having to lead Mordecai through the city on the king's horse. At Esther's second feast, she told the king about Haman's plot against her people, and Haman was put to death. A new decree allowed the Jews to defend themselves, and they kept the days of Purim with feasting and gifts to the poor.
d151-crown.why: The story turns on small moments and brave words, with a feast to remember it.

d152-ruins.title: Job loses everything
d152-ruins.story: Esther ends with a short note about King Xerxes. Then the book of Job begins with a man in the land of Uz who was honest and feared God, with a large family and many animals. In a single day messengers brought news that his oxen, sheep, camels and servants were gone and that his children had died in a storm. Job tore his robe, fell to the ground and said, "The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away." Later sores covered his body, and he sat in the ashes while three friends came and sat with him in silence for seven days.
d152-ruins.why: Job's friends did their best work when they simply sat with him, before they began to explain.

d153-tent_camp.title: The friends begin to speak
d153-tent_camp.story: Job answered Eliphaz, who had hinted that Job must have done something wrong. He said his grief would outweigh the sand of the seas and that his friends were as faithless as streams that run dry. He told God his days were swifter than a weaver's shuttle. Bildad then said God does not twist justice, and if Job were pure God would restore him.
d153-tent_camp.why: The friends offered tidy answers, and Job pushed back that suffering is not always so simple.

d154-wilderness.title: How can a man argue with God
d154-wilderness.story: Job agreed that God is wise and powerful and asked how a man can be right before him. He said God moves mountains and made the Bear and Orion, yet no one can summon him to court. Job longed for someone to stand between him and God and settle the matter. Then Zophar, the third friend, told Job that God was asking less of him than his wrongs deserved, and that if he turned back to God, he would feel secure.
d154-wilderness.why: Job's honest wondering about whether God would hear him is treated as part of faith, not its failure.

d155-stump_shoot.title: A felled tree may sprout
d155-stump_shoot.story: Job told his friends he was not less wise than they were, and he spoke of God's power over nations and the deep. He said that there is hope for a tree, since if it is cut down it will sprout again, but a person who dies lies down and does not rise, and he asked, "When a man dies, will he live again?" Eliphaz replied sharply that Job's own words condemned him. Job could find little hope, but he kept speaking to God.
d155-stump_shoot.why: The image of a stump sprouting is one of hope, and Job holds it up even while doubting it applies to him.

d156-house.title: Miserable comforters
d156-house.story: Job answered that he had heard such things before and called his friends miserable comforters. He said that if he were in their place, he would strengthen them with words, not lecture them. He felt that God had worn him out, and yet he said his witness was in heaven. Bildad answered with a stern picture of how the wicked fare, and Job's friends kept pressing him.
d156-house.why: Comfort is more than words, and the passage shows what unhelpful comfort feels like.

d157-scroll.title: I know my Redeemer lives
d157-scroll.story: Job asked his friends how long they would crush him with words. He said his family and friends had turned from him and he looked like skin and bones. Then he wished his words were inscribed in a book and declared, "But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end he will stand upon the earth." Zophar answered with another speech about the fate of the wicked, and Job said that sometimes the wicked prosper.
d157-scroll.why: In the middle of his worst night, Job spoke a line of hope that readers have repeated for centuries.

d158-signpost.title: Job longs to find God
d158-signpost.story: Eliphaz accused Job of specific wrongs with no evidence and urged him to make peace with God. Job said he wished he knew where to find God, so that he could lay out his case, but that when he looked east, west, north and south, God was not to be seen. He still said that when God had tested him, he would come out as gold. Bildad said briefly that no one is pure before God.
d158-signpost.why: Job did not pretend that everything was fine, and he stayed honest while he waited to hear from God.

d159-cave.title: Where wisdom is found
d159-cave.story: Job described the work of miners who dig deep into the earth to find silver, iron and gems, in places where no bird of prey has seen. Then he asked, "But where can wisdom be found?" He said it cannot be bought with gold, and the sea and the deep say it is not in them. God alone knows the way to it. The poem ends, "The fear of the Lord, that is wisdom." He then remembered his earlier days, when he was honored and helped the poor.
d159-cave.why: The poem suggests wisdom is something to be received with reverence and not mined or bought.

d160-city_gate.title: Job's oath of innocence
d160-city_gate.story: Job said that men younger than he, who once respected him, now mocked him. He swore a long oath, saying he had not treated servants unjustly, not ignored the poor and not trusted in gold. He wished that someone would hear him and that the Almighty would answer. In chapter 32 the three friends stopped, because Job was sure of his own innocence.
d160-city_gate.why: Job's long list shows how he thought a good life ought to look, treating other people fairly.

d161-oak.title: Elihu speaks
d161-oak.story: Elihu, a younger man, kept speaking to Job. He said God speaks to people in one way and another, sometimes through dreams or pain, and that a messenger may stand by someone to show them what is right. He insisted that God is just and does not do wrong, and that he hears the cry of the poor.
d161-oak.why: Elihu's speech opens the way for God to speak, and it reminds us that wisdom can come from unexpected people.

d162-whirlwind.title: The voice from the whirlwind
d162-whirlwind.story: After many speeches, the Lord answered Job from a storm. God asked him, "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?" and went on with questions about the sea, the morning, the snow, the stars and the animals. The questions were not an explanation of Job's suffering. They showed him how large and carefully made the world is, and how much lay beyond what he could see.
d162-whirlwind.why: The answer was an invitation to look at the vastness of the world and trust the one who made it.

d163-fish.title: Wild creatures and Leviathan
d163-fish.story: God kept speaking from the storm, asking Job about wild goats, the wild donkey, the ox and the ostrich, and the horse that charges into battle with no fear. He pointed to the hawk and the eagle. Job could only say that he was insignificant and put his hand over his mouth. Then God described Behemoth, a huge creature that eats grass, and Leviathan, a sea creature so fierce that no one dares stir it up.
d163-fish.why: The creatures remind us that much of the world runs by a wisdom we did not design.

d164-rivertree.title: Job restored and the tree by the streams
d164-rivertree.story: Job answered the Lord and said he had spoken of things he did not understand, and now his eyes had seen God. He took back his words, and God told his friends they had not spoken rightly, and Job prayed for them. The Lord restored Job's fortunes, doubled what he had and gave him seven sons and three daughters. Psalms then begins with the picture of a blessed person who delights in the law and is like a tree planted by streams of water.
d164-rivertree.why: Job prayed for the friends who had wronged him, and Psalm 1 follows with a picture of steady, rooted life.

d165-stars.title: When I consider the heavens
d165-stars.story: These psalms are short songs of trust and plea. In Psalm 6 David asks to be healed and not to be rebuked in anger, and in Psalm 8 he looks up at the night sky and says, "When I behold Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars," and asks, "What is man that You are mindful of him?" He is amazed that people are given care over the animals and the earth. Other psalms in this group cry for help against enemies and give thanks for justice.
d165-stars.why: Looking up at the stars can make us feel small and also notice how much we are cared for.

d166-mountain.title: Who may dwell on your holy hill
d166-mountain.story: This stretch of psalms moves between asking for help and speaking trust. Psalm 13 asks, "How long, O LORD?" and then ends with a song of trust. Psalm 15 asks who may live on God's holy hill and answers with honest speech, fairness and keeping promises. Psalm 18 is David's song of thanks for rescue, calling God his rock and fortress. Other psalms in this group pray for refuge and speak of God as a shelter.
d166-mountain.why: The psalms allow honest questions and say plainly what a good life looks like.

d167-sun_moon.title: The heavens declare
d167-sun_moon.story: Psalm 19 begins, "The heavens declare the glory of God," and says the sky speaks day and night with no words. It then turns to God's law, saying it revives the soul and gives joy and light to the eyes. Psalm 22 begins with "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" and moves from deep distress to praise. Psalms 20 and 21 pray for the king and give thanks for his victories.
d167-sun_moon.why: The psalms hold wonder at the sky and hurt in the dark side by side.

d168-pasture.title: The Lord is my shepherd
d168-pasture.story: This short psalm, described as a psalm of David, pictures God as a shepherd and the writer as a sheep who lacks nothing. The shepherd leads him to green pastures and quiet waters, restores his soul and guides him along right paths. Even in the darkest valley, he says, he will not be afraid, because the shepherd is with him. The psalm ends with a table prepared, goodness following him all his life, and a home in the house of the Lord.
d168-pasture.why: People have turned to it in grief and in fear for centuries as a reminder that they are not alone.

d169-harp.title: Sing a new song
d169-harp.story: These psalms are songs of thanks and joy. Psalm 30 says weeping may stay for the night but joy comes in the morning, and Psalm 32 tells of the relief of being forgiven. Psalm 33 invites everyone to sing a new song with skill and shouts of joy. Psalm 34 says, "Taste and see that the Lord is good," and says the Lord is close to the broken hearted.
d169-harp.why: These songs show gratitude as something to be sung and a blessing for the hurting.

d170-oasis.title: The fountain of life
d170-oasis.story: Psalm 35 asks for help against enemies, and Psalm 36 speaks of God's steady love reaching to the heavens. It says, "With you is the fountain of life; in your light we see light." Psalm 37 tells the reader not to fret over those who do wrong and to trust the Lord, be patient and do good. It says the meek will inherit the land and that the Lord holds up the one whose steps he delights in.
d170-oasis.why: The psalm offers calm for an anxious mind and a reminder that wrongdoers do not have the last word.

d171-stream.title: As the deer pants for water
d171-stream.story: Psalm 42 opens, "As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after you, O God." The writer is far from the temple and tearful, remembering earlier days of worship. He asks his own soul why it is cast down and tells it to hope in God. Psalm 43 repeats the question and the hope, asking God to send light and truth.
d171-stream.why: The writer talks to his own soul with honesty and turns it toward hope.

d172-city_wall.title: Walk around Zion
d172-city_wall.story: These psalms speak of God as a refuge. Psalm 46 says God is a refuge and strength, an ever present help in trouble, and says, "Be still, and know that I am God." Psalm 47 invites all peoples to clap their hands. Psalm 48 speaks of the city of Zion and invites readers to walk around it, count its towers and tell the next generation. Psalm 49 reminds the rich that wealth cannot buy a person's life.
d172-city_wall.why: The psalm of stillness is a good one to read when the world feels loud.

d173-basin.title: Create in me a clean heart
d173-basin.story: Psalm 51 is a prayer of David after Nathan confronted him about Bathsheba. He asks God to have mercy, to wash him and to cleanse him of sin. He prays, "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me," and asks not to be sent away from God's presence. He says God does not want only offerings, but a broken and humble spirit. Other psalms here include a psalm of judgment and a cry for help.
d173-basin.why: The psalm gives words to anyone who needs to say sorry and start over.

d174-cave.title: In the cave
d174-cave.story: Psalm 57 is described as a prayer of David when he fled from Saul into the cave. He says he takes refuge in the shadow of God's wings until the danger has passed. Psalm 56 says, "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you," and Psalm 61 asks, "Lead me to the rock that is higher than I." The psalms here pass from fear to confidence.
d174-cave.why: A cave is a hard place to sing from, and the psalms show prayer starting there.

d175-wilderness.title: Thirsting in a dry land
d175-wilderness.story: Psalm 63 is a prayer of David in the wilderness of Judah. He says, "O God, You are my God. Earnestly I seek You; my soul thirsts for You. My body yearns for You in a dry and weary land without water." He remembers seeing God in the sanctuary and says God's love is better than life. He thinks of God through the watches of the night. Psalm 62 says rest in God alone, and Psalm 68 praises God as a father to orphans.
d175-wilderness.why: The psalm speaks to dry seasons of life, saying that feeling thirsty is itself a way of seeking God.

d176-stream.title: Sinking in deep waters
d176-stream.story: Psalm 69 begins, "Save me, O God, for the waters are up to my neck." The writer says he sinks in deep mire and is worn out from calling, and he has been mocked for his faith. He asks for rescue and trusts that God hears the needy. The psalm ends with praise. Psalm 71 is an older person's prayer, asking God not to leave him in old age.
d176-stream.why: The psalm says plainly when someone is drowning in trouble, and still manages to turn toward praise in the end.

d177-crown.title: A king's justice
d177-crown.story: Psalm 72 is a prayer for the king, asking that he would rule with justice and help the poor. It asks that he would rescue the needy who cry out, and the vulnerable who have no one to help them. It pictures grain on the hills and prosperity for all. Psalms 73 to 76 follow, including one writer who nearly slipped when he saw the wicked prosper, until he went into God's house and understood.
d177-crown.why: What the psalm asks of a king is care for the poor, and it holds leaders to that.

d178-redsea.title: Your way through the sea
d178-redsea.story: Psalm 77 begins with a person in trouble who cannot sleep. He remembers the old days and asks if God's love has faded. Then he turns his thoughts to what God did before, and says, "Your path led through the sea, your way through the mighty waters," and says God led his people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron. Psalm 78 tells the history of Israel, from the sea and the cloud to the choice of David as shepherd.
d178-redsea.why: When the present feels dark, remembering how help came before can steady a person.

d179-vineyard.title: The vine from Egypt
d179-vineyard.story: These psalms mix sorrow and hope. Psalm 79 cries out over a ruined Jerusalem and asks for help. Psalm 80 pictures Israel as a vine that God brought out of Egypt, planted and watched grow until it filled the land. The psalm asks why its walls are broken and prays, "Restore us, O God, and cause your face to shine upon us, that we may be saved." Psalms 81 and 82 call people back and ask for justice for the weak.
d179-vineyard.why: The vine picture says a people can be tended and still ask to be restored.

d180-tabernacle.title: How lovely is your dwelling
d180-tabernacle.story: Psalm 84 says, "How lovely is your dwelling place, O Lord of Hosts!" and speaks of how even a sparrow finds a home near the altar. It says one day in God's courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. Psalm 88 is a prayer from deep trouble that ends in darkness, with no easy answer. Psalm 89 remembers God's covenant with David and sings of his steady love.
d180-tabernacle.why: The psalms here make room for both a deep longing for God and sorrow that stays unresolved for a while.

d181-sundial.title: Teach us to number our days
d181-sundial.story: Psalm 90 is a prayer of Moses. It says, "Lord, you have been our dwelling place through all generations," and compares human life to grass that sprouts in the morning and withers by evening. It asks, "So teach us to number our days, that we may present a heart of wisdom," and asks God to satisfy people with his love each morning. Psalm 91 speaks of shelter in the Most High, and Psalm 92 of giving thanks.
d181-sundial.why: Remembering that our days are few can help us spend them with care and gratitude instead of in hurry.

d182-shofar.title: Come, let us sing
d182-shofar.story: These psalms call everyone to praise. Psalm 95 says, "Come, let us sing for joy to the Lord," and calls people to kneel and not harden their hearts. Psalm 96 says, "Sing to the Lord a new song," and invites all nations and the whole earth. Psalm 98 adds the sound of trumpets and horns, and the seas and rivers join in. Psalm 99 calls the Lord holy.
d182-shofar.why: The invitation here is wide open, with the whole earth asked to sing and nobody left out of the song.

d183-garden.title: The creation hymn
d183-garden.story: Psalm 100 invites all the earth to shout for joy and come into God's presence with thanks. Psalm 103 says, "Bless the Lord, O my soul," and lists his benefits: he forgives, heals and satisfies, and as far as the east is from the west, so far he removes our wrongs. Psalm 104 praises God for the world, from the springs in the valleys to the birds, the wild goats, the sea creatures and the moon that marks the seasons.
d183-garden.why: The creation hymn invites us to notice the world as a gift, with room for every creature.

d184-manna_quail.title: Remember his wonders
d184-manna_quail.story: Psalm 105 tells Israel's story as a list of God's wonders: the promise to Abraham, Joseph sold and later raised up, the plagues, and food in the desert. Psalm 106 tells the same story again, but this time it admits how often the people forgot, grumbled and turned away. Even so, the psalm says God remembered his covenant and heard their cry. It ends with a prayer to be gathered from the nations.
d184-manna_quail.why: It is honest memory: the psalmist gives thanks for what God did and owns up to what the people did, and both belong in the story.

d185-ship.title: Those who go down to the sea in ships
d185-ship.story: Psalm 107 gathers people who were lost, locked up, sick or caught at sea, and each group cries to the Lord in trouble. The sailors go down to the sea in ships, and a storm lifts the waves until they are at their wits' end. The Lord calms the storm to a whisper and brings them to the harbor they were heading for. After each rescue comes the same refrain: let them give thanks for his steadfast love. Psalms 108 and 109 follow with a prayer for help.
d185-ship.why: Everyone has a storm sooner or later, and this psalm says that crying out is the right thing to do, and that thanks is the right thing to do afterward.

d186-crown.title: Sit at my right hand
d186-crown.story: Psalm 110 is a short royal song in which the Lord says to the king, "Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet." It also calls him a priest forever, in the line of Melchizedek. The next psalms are songs of praise: the Lord lifts the poor from the dust and the childless woman is given a home. Psalm 116 is one person's thanks that God heard them when death was near.
d186-crown.why: These psalms praise a God who stoops down to lift up the lowly, which is a good thing to remember when you feel small.

d187-lamp.title: A lamp to my feet
d187-lamp.story: Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, a poem in praise of God's word. It is an acrostic, arranged by the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, and every verse in a section of eight begins with that section's letter. The writer uses many names for God's word, such as law, commands, decrees and promises. He says it is a lamp for his feet and a light for his path, and he asks God to help him keep it, even in trouble.
d187-lamp.why: It shows Scripture as daily guidance: a lamp lights the next few steps, not the whole road at once.

d188-signpost.title: The songs of ascents begin
d188-signpost.story: Psalm 120 is the first of the songs of ascents, short songs often linked with pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. It opens in distress, with a person who is tired of lies and of living among people who hate peace. The writer says, "I am in favor of peace; but when I speak, they want war." Only the first step of the journey has been taken, and it begins in an honest cry for help.
d188-signpost.why: Even a journey toward God can begin with weariness, and the psalms let you start the walk just as you are.

d189-mountain.title: I lift my eyes to the hills
d189-mountain.story: Psalm 121 begins with a pilgrim lifting his eyes to the hills and asking where help will come from. The answer is that help comes from the Lord, who made heaven and earth, who does not slumber and who keeps watch over your going out and your coming in. Psalm 122 is the joy of finally arriving, "I was glad when they said to me, let us go to the house of the Lord." Psalms 123 and 124 turn to praying for mercy and thanking God for rescue.
d189-mountain.why: It is a comfort for travelers and worriers alike: the one watching over you does not get tired and does not look away.

d190-house.title: Unless the Lord builds the house
d190-house.story: Psalm 127 says that unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Psalm 128 pictures a family eating together around the table, and Psalm 133 says how good and pleasant it is when people live together in unity. Psalm 130 cries out from the depths and waits for the Lord like watchmen waiting for the morning. Psalm 131 is a quiet child resting against its mother, and Psalm 134 tells those who serve at night to bless the Lord.
d190-house.why: These pilgrim songs treat ordinary things like work, home, waiting and rest as places where God is present.

d191-harp.title: By the rivers of Babylon
d191-harp.story: Psalm 136 repeats the line "His loving devotion endures forever" after each thing God has done, from making the heavens to bringing Israel out of Egypt. Then comes Psalm 137, written in exile: by the rivers of Babylon the people sat down and wept as they remembered Zion, and they hung their harps on the willows. Their captors asked for a happy song, and they could not sing it. The psalm is raw and ends with an angry cry. Psalms 138 to 140 return to thanks and prayer.
d191-harp.why: The Bible makes room for grief and anger as well as praise, so you do not have to hide your hardest feelings from God.

d192-altar.title: Let my prayer rise like incense
d192-altar.story: Psalm 141 is an evening prayer: "May my prayer be set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering." The writer asks to be kept from wrong and to be corrected by good people. Psalm 142 is a prayer from a cave, and Psalm 143 asks God to teach him to do his will. The book then climbs into praise: Psalm 145 praises God's greatness, and Psalm 147 says he builds up Jerusalem, gathers the outcasts and heals the brokenhearted.
d192-altar.why: Prayer does not have to be polished. A short cry at the end of the day is still counted by God.

d193-treasury.title: Seeking wisdom like treasure
d193-treasury.story: The Psalms end in a burst of praise: Psalm 148 calls on sun, moon, mountains, animals and all people to praise the Lord, and Psalm 150 says let everything that has breath praise him, with trumpet, harp, dance and cymbals. Then Proverbs begins, saying its purpose is to teach wisdom and discipline. Wisdom is pictured as a woman calling in the streets, and the writer says that if you search for wisdom like silver and hidden treasure, you will find the fear of the Lord.
d193-treasury.why: Wisdom is something you can look for on purpose, and the search itself is part of what the Bible calls a good life.

d194-signpost.title: Straight paths
d194-signpost.story: Proverbs 3 gives a father's advice: trust in the Lord with all your heart, do not lean on your own understanding, and in all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight. The father also says not to hold back good from those who deserve it, and he praises wisdom as worth more than silver. Chapters 4 and 5 add a warning to guard your heart, because everything you do flows from it, and to stay faithful to your own spouse.
d194-signpost.why: A hard decision is easier to face if you start from trust and not from having everything figured out.

d195-ant_trail.title: Go to the ant
d195-ant_trail.story: In Proverbs 6, the writer says to the lazy person, "Walk in the manner of the ant, O slacker; observe its ways and become wise." The ant has no ruler, yet she stores up food in summer. The chapter also warns against guaranteeing a stranger's debt and lists things the Lord hates, such as lying and spilling innocent blood. In chapter 8, Wisdom speaks again and says she was beside God when he made the heavens and the earth, rejoicing in his world.
d195-ant_trail.why: Wisdom can be learned from small, ordinary things, even an ant, if you are willing to watch.

d196-house.title: Wisdom builds her house
d196-house.story: Proverbs 9 sets two women side by side. Wisdom builds her house, sets her table with meat and wine, and sends her servants to call out to the simple, "Come, eat my bread." Folly sits at her door and calls to the same people with stolen water and secret bread, but her guests end up among the dead. Chapters 10 and 11 then begin a long run of short sayings, such as the person of integrity walking securely and a generous person being enriched.
d196-house.why: Every day offers two invitations, and this chapter asks which table you are going to sit at.

d197-well.title: A wise teaching is a fountain
d197-well.story: These chapters are short sayings, set side by side. Whoever works the land will have plenty of food, but chasing fantasies shows a lack of sense, and the teaching of the wise is a fountain of life. Whoever walks with the wise will become wise. Proverbs 14:12 says there is a way that seems right to a person, but its end is the way to death. Other sayings note that a kind word cheers an anxious heart, and that righteousness lifts up a nation.
d197-well.why: Many proverbs sound simple, but they ask you to look at your work, speech and choices and notice where they lead.

d198-lamp.title: A gentle answer
d198-lamp.story: Proverbs 15 opens with a saying many people know: "A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger." It goes on to say a cheerful look brings joy and that better is a little with the fear of the Lord than great treasure with trouble. Chapter 16 turns to planning: a person plans their way, but the Lord establishes their steps. It also says pride goes before destruction, and that pleasant words are like honey.
d198-lamp.why: You get to choose how you answer. A gentle word is often stronger than a loud one.

d199-watchtower.title: The name of the Lord is a strong tower
d199-watchtower.story: Proverbs 18:10 says the name of the Lord is a strong tower, and the righteous run into it and are safe. The same chapters are full of sayings about people: a friend loves at all times, and there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother. They also warn that a person who answers before listening shows folly, and that the tongue has the power of life and death. Chapter 20 notes that many say they are loyal, but a faithful person is hard to find.
d199-watchtower.why: A strong tower is there when you run to it, and so is a good friend, so it helps to learn who to run to.

d200-city_gate.title: Justice at the gate
d200-city_gate.story: Proverbs 21 and 22 gather sayings about how people should treat each other. To do what is right and just is more pleasing to the Lord than sacrifice. Whoever shuts their ear to the cry of the poor will cry out and not be answered. A good name is to be chosen over great riches, and rich and poor have this in common: the Lord made them both. Chapter 22 also says to train up a child in the way he should go.
d200-city_gate.why: Justice and a good name are built in small, daily acts of honesty and care, not just in big public moments.

d201-scroll.title: Proverbs copied by Hezekiah's men
d201-scroll.story: Proverbs 25 begins, "These are additional proverbs of Solomon, which were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah." It shows that people were gathering and preserving these sayings long after Solomon. The chapters include some vivid images: a word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver, and if your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat. Chapter 23 warns against drinking too much, and chapter 24 says even the righteous may fall seven times and rise again.
d201-scroll.why: Wisdom is handed down. Someone copied these sayings out so that people long afterward could still read them.

d202-plowshare.title: Iron sharpens iron
d202-plowshare.story: These chapters contain pairs of sayings. Proverbs 26 warns about fools, who repeat their folly as a dog returns to its vomit, and gossips whose words are like tasty morsels. Proverbs 27 offers a picture of friendship: "As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another." It also says not to boast about tomorrow, since you do not know what a day may bring. Chapter 28 says whoever works their land will have plenty of food, and the one who hides sin will not prosper.
d202-plowshare.why: Good friends make you better. This proverb suggests the people around you are shaping you, and you are shaping them.

d203-vineyard.title: The woman of strength
d203-vineyard.story: Proverbs 30 is the sayings of Agur, who admits his limits and prays, "Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion." He names things too wonderful for him to understand, including the way of an eagle in the sky. Proverbs 31 records what King Lemuel's mother taught him, including a portrait of a capable woman. She works with willing hands, plants a vineyard, helps the poor, and speaks with wisdom and kindness. Her family praises her.
d203-vineyard.why: The book of Proverbs ends by praising everyday strength: a person who works well, speaks kindly and is generous.

d204-sundial.title: A time for everything
d204-sundial.story: Ecclesiastes opens with the Teacher saying everything is a vapor, like breath, and asking what a person gains from all their labor under the sun. He tried wisdom, pleasure, building projects and wealth, and each one left him asking what it was for. Chapter 3 then says there is a time for everything: a time to be born and a time to die, a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance. God has also set eternity in the human heart.
d204-sundial.why: The Teacher is honest about how short life feels, and he suggests that seasons come and go and each one has its place.

d205-synagogue.title: Guard your steps in God's house
d205-synagogue.story: The Teacher says to guard your steps when you go to the house of God, and to draw near to listen rather than to offer a fool's sacrifice. Let your words before God be few. He observes that whoever loves money will never have enough, and that it is a gift of God to enjoy your work and what you have been given. In chapter 7 he says it is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting, because that is the end of everyone.
d205-synagogue.why: Slowing down in worship and in speech leaves more room to listen, and a quiet heart often hears best.

d206-stream.title: Cast your bread upon the waters
d206-stream.story: The Teacher says to go, eat your bread with joy and enjoy life with the people you love, because you do not know when your time will come. He also says, "Cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you will find it again," and to be generous and take risks, since nobody can know what will succeed. The book ends with advice to remember your Creator in the days of your youth. Song of Songs 1 then begins a love poem between two people.
d206-stream.why: Be generous and enjoy the good things now, and do not let the years slip by without noticing where your life comes from.

d207-garden_door.title: The garden and the door
d207-garden_door.story: Song of Songs is a book of love poetry between a woman and a man. In chapter 2 she hears him say that winter is past and the flowers have appeared on the earth. In chapter 4 he calls her a garden locked, a fountain sealed. In chapter 5 he knocks at her door at night, and she is slow to open, and by the time she does he has gone, and she goes out searching for him through the city. The poem follows longing and delight in each other.
d207-garden_door.why: The Bible includes a book that simply celebrates love between two people, which says that human love and longing are good gifts.

d208-mountain.title: The mountain of the Lord
d208-mountain.story: Song of Songs 8 says love is strong as death and that many waters cannot quench it, and that love cannot be bought. Then Isaiah begins. Isaiah 1 opens with the Lord accusing his people of empty worship and calling them to stop doing evil and learn to do good, to seek justice and help the oppressed. In chapter 2 Isaiah sees a day when the mountain of the Lord's house will be raised and nations will stream to it, saying, "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord."
d208-mountain.why: Love cannot be bought, and God cares more about how we treat the oppressed than about showy worship.

d209-throne.title: Isaiah sees the throne
d209-throne.story: In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the Lord sitting on a high and lofty throne, with the edges of his robe filling the temple. Seraphim, winged beings, called to one another, "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts." Isaiah said he was a man of unclean lips, and one of them touched his mouth with a burning coal from the altar and told him his guilt was taken away. Then he heard the Lord ask, "Whom shall I send?" and answered, "Here am I. Send me!"
d209-throne.why: Isaiah is forgiven first and sent second, which is a pattern for anyone who feels unfit to speak or serve.

d210-stump_shoot.title: A shoot from the stump of Jesse
d210-stump_shoot.story: Isaiah promises that people who walked in darkness have seen a great light, and that a child will be born to them with the names Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father and Prince of Peace. Chapter 11 pictures a shoot growing from the stump of Jesse, David's father, as if a cut-down family tree is not finished yet. The Spirit of the Lord rests on him, and the wolf lives with the lamb and the leopard lies down with the young goat. Christians read this as pointing to Jesus.
d210-stump_shoot.why: Hope can start small. A green shoot from an old stump is a picture of peace that grows out of what looked finished.

d211-well.title: Wells of salvation
d211-well.story: Isaiah 12 is a short song of thanks: "Surely God is my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid." It says with joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation. After it come oracles about nations around Israel, including Babylon, Assyria, Philistia and Moab, each told that God sees what they do and that no power lasts forever. Chapter 14 speaks about the fall of a proud king of Babylon who thought himself above everyone.
d211-well.why: Between the warnings, this chapter gives a song of thanks, and it suggests that trust is like drawing water from a well.

d212-watchtower.title: The watchman on the tower
d212-watchtower.story: Isaiah is told to take off his sackcloth and sandals and go about naked and barefoot for three years, as a sign that Egypt and Cush would be led away captive. In chapter 21 a watchman is stationed on the tower, and someone asks him, "Watchman, what is left of the night?" He answers, "Morning has come, but also the night." Chapter 22 describes Jerusalem in a panic as enemies approach, and the people choose feasting over repentance, saying, "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die."
d212-watchtower.why: Watching and waiting are real work. The watchman still answers honestly, even when the news is mixed.

d213-table.title: A feast on the mountain
d213-table.story: Isaiah 25 says the Lord of hosts will prepare a feast of rich food and fine wine on the mountain for all peoples. He will swallow up death forever and wipe away tears from all faces. The people say, "Surely this is our God; we have waited for Him, and He has saved us." Chapter 26 adds a song of trust: "You will keep in perfect peace the steadfast of mind, because he trusts in You."
d213-table.why: Isaiah looks ahead to a table where everyone is welcome and no one weeps, and he offers it as a reason to keep hoping now.

d214-cornerstone.title: The cornerstone in Zion
d214-cornerstone.story: Isaiah 28 says the Lord is laying in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation, and whoever believes will not be in haste. It follows warnings about leaders who made a covenant with death, and about people who honor God with their lips while their hearts are far away. In chapter 30 Isaiah says that in returning and rest you will be saved, and that the Lord waits to be gracious to you.
d214-cornerstone.why: A strong foundation is better than a hasty fix, and God offers to be that foundation.

d215-ruins.title: Edom made desolate
d215-ruins.story: Isaiah 31 warns people against going down to Egypt for help and relying on horses and chariots, because they did not look to the Holy One of Israel. Chapters 32 and 33 promise a righteous king and say that a quiet, secure home will come, though the land mourns for now. Chapter 34 turns to Edom, a neighboring nation, which is told it will become a wasteland, a place of ruins where wild animals live.
d215-ruins.why: These chapters warn against trusting in strength that cannot save, and they speak plainly about what happens to proud powers.

d216-desert_bloom.title: The desert blooms
d216-desert_bloom.story: Isaiah 35 says the desert and the dry land will be glad, and the wilderness will rejoice and blossom like the crocus. The weak hands will be strengthened, the eyes of the blind opened, the lame will leap like a deer, and a highway called the Way of Holiness will lead the ransomed home to Zion. Then chapters 36 to 38 tell how Assyria threatened Jerusalem, and King Hezekiah, who fell ill and was told to prepare to die, prayed and was given fifteen more years.
d216-desert_bloom.why: These chapters picture dry places blooming and weak hands being strengthened, and they remind us that a prayer from a sickbed was heard.

d217-wilderness.title: A voice in the wilderness
d217-wilderness.story: Isaiah 40 begins, "Comfort, comfort my people, says your God." A voice cries out, "Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness; make a straight highway for our God in the desert." The grass withers and the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever. The chapter ends with the promise that those who wait for the Lord will renew their strength, mount up with wings like eagles, run and not be weary. The Gospels later connect the voice in the wilderness with John the Baptist.
d217-wilderness.why: When you are worn out, the invitation is to wait and let God renew your strength.

d218-stream.title: Water on the thirsty land
d218-stream.story: Isaiah 43 says, "When you pass through the waters, I will be with you, and when you go through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you." God says he has called his people by name and that they are precious in his sight. In chapter 44 he promises to pour water on the thirsty land and streams on dry ground, and to pour out his Spirit on their children. Chapter 45 names Cyrus, a Persian king, as someone God will use to let the exiles go home.
d218-stream.why: God promises company in hard places rather than a way around them, and he knows each of us by name.

d219-city_wall.title: The fall of Babylon
d219-city_wall.story: Isaiah 46 says that the gods of Babylon, Bel and Nebo, are carried on tired animals, while the true God carries his people from birth to old age. Chapter 47 says Babylon, once called the mistress of kingdoms, will be brought down and sit in the dust. Chapter 48 tells the exiles, "Leave Babylon!" and in chapter 49 the servant is made a light for the nations. When Zion says the Lord has forgotten her, he says a mother may forget her nursing child, but he will not forget her.
d219-city_wall.why: Empires that look permanent fall, but the promise is that you are not forgotten.

d220-lamb.title: The suffering servant
d220-lamb.story: Isaiah 50 to 53 speak of a servant of the Lord who gives his back to those who strike him and does not hide his face. Isaiah 53 says he was despised and rejected, a man of sorrows. It says he was pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities, and led like a lamb to the slaughter, and that by his wounds we are healed. Christians read this as pointing to Jesus, while many Jewish readers understand the servant as Israel. Chapter 55 invites everyone who is thirsty to come to the waters.
d220-lamb.why: The text speaks of someone who carried the pain of others, and then it ends with an open invitation to come and drink.

d221-sun_moon.title: Arise, shine
d221-sun_moon.story: Isaiah 56 says God's house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples, and that foreigners and those who had been excluded will be welcomed. In chapter 58 the people ask why God does not notice their fasting, and he says the fast he wants is to loose the bonds of injustice, share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house. Chapter 60 begins, "Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD rises upon you."
d221-sun_moon.why: True faith shows up in how you treat people who are hungry or left out, and then the light follows.

d222-scroll.title: Good news to the poor
d222-scroll.story: In Isaiah 61, the servant says, "The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor." He is sent to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to captives and to comfort all who mourn, giving them beauty for ashes. Jesus later read these words in the synagogue at Nazareth. In chapter 65 God says he is creating new heavens and a new earth, where people will build houses and live in them, and the wolf and the lamb will feed together.
d222-scroll.why: The good news in these chapters is aimed first at the poor and brokenhearted, and it ends with a world made new.

d223-well.title: Broken cisterns
d223-well.story: Isaiah ends with God saying heaven is his throne and earth his footstool, yet he looks to the humble and contrite, and will comfort his people as a mother comforts her child. Then the book of Jeremiah begins. The Lord says he knew Jeremiah before he was formed in the womb and calls him as a prophet to the nations, and Jeremiah says he is only a youth. In chapter 2 the Lord says his people have forsaken him, the fountain of living water, and dug cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water.
d223-well.why: It is a warning not to give up what truly satisfies for things that leak, and a reminder that God calls people who feel too young or small.

d224-whirlwind.title: The foe like a whirlwind
d224-whirlwind.story: Jeremiah 3 calls the people of Israel to return, and says, "Return, O faithless children, and I will heal your faithlessness." In chapter 4 a message comes of a foe from the north, a destroyer moving like a whirlwind with horses swifter than eagles. Jeremiah is anguished at what he sees, crying that his heart is pounding within him. In chapter 5 God asks whether anyone in Jerusalem acts justly and seeks truth, and says he would pardon the city for one such person.
d224-whirlwind.why: The warning is painful, but the call to return still stands, and God is looking for even one honest person.

d225-siege.title: The siege of Jerusalem
d225-siege.story: Jeremiah 6 warns that enemies will soon besiege Jerusalem. The people say "Peace, peace" when there is no peace, and the prophet says they have healed the wound of the people lightly. Jeremiah stands at the gate of the Lord's house in chapter 7 and says not to trust in the words "This is the temple of the Lord," but to truly change your ways, treat each other justly and not oppress the foreigner, the orphan or the widow. Chapter 8 asks, "Is there no balm in Gilead?"
d225-siege.why: A building does not keep a people safe. Honest change and care for the vulnerable matter more than a comfortable slogan.

d226-golden_calf.title: Idols like scarecrows
d226-golden_calf.story: Jeremiah 10 compares the idols of the nations to scarecrows in a cucumber field, which cannot speak and must be carried because they cannot walk. By contrast, the Lord is the true God, who made the earth by his power. Jeremiah is also shown weeping: "Oh, that my head were a spring of water, and my eyes a fountain of tears! I would weep day and night over the slain daughter of my people." Chapter 12 has him ask God honestly why the wicked prosper.
d226-golden_calf.why: Jeremiah's grief shows that a prophet can love the people he warns, and he is allowed to bring hard questions to God.

d227-cave.title: The linen belt in the rock
d227-cave.story: The Lord tells Jeremiah to buy a linen belt, wear it, and then bury it in a crevice of a rock by the Euphrates. After many days he digs it up and finds it ruined and good for nothing. God says that is what he will do to the pride of Judah. In chapter 14 a drought grips the land, and in chapter 16 Jeremiah is told not to marry or attend funerals as a sign of what is coming. Yet chapter 16 also promises that the people will one day be brought back.
d227-cave.why: The story uses a spoiled belt to make a point: what is meant to cling to God can be ruined when it is left alone.

d228-potter.title: The potter at the wheel
d228-potter.story: God tells Jeremiah to go down to the potter's house. There he watches the potter working at the wheel, and the vessel he is making is spoiled in his hand, so the potter reshapes it into another vessel as seemed good to him. God says, "Just like clay in the potter's hand, so are you in My hand, O house of Israel." If a nation turns from evil, God will relent. Chapter 20 shows the cost of Jeremiah's work, as he is beaten and put in stocks, and he laments that he was born.
d228-potter.why: It is a picture of a God who can reshape what looks ruined, and an honest look at how heavy a calling can feel.

d229-stump_shoot.title: A righteous Branch
d229-stump_shoot.story: Jeremiah 21 begins with King Zedekiah asking Jeremiah to seek the Lord about the Babylonian attack. Chapter 23 is aimed at kings and prophets who have scattered the sheep, and the Lord says he will gather his flock and raise up shepherds who will care for them. He promises, "Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and He will reign wisely as King and will administer justice and righteousness in the land." Christians read this as pointing to Jesus.
d229-stump_shoot.why: Poor leaders can scatter people, and these chapters hold out the hope of a ruler who is truly just.

d230-fig_tree.title: Two baskets of figs
d230-fig_tree.story: After Babylon carried off many people from Jerusalem, Jeremiah is shown two baskets of figs set before the temple. One has very good figs, and the other has very bad figs, too rotten to eat. The Lord says the good figs are the exiles in Babylon, whom he will watch over and bring back, and the bad figs are King Zedekiah and those who stayed. In chapter 26 Jeremiah is nearly killed for his warnings, and in chapter 27 he wears a yoke to show that the nations should serve Babylon.
d230-fig_tree.why: The story overturns what people expected: God had not given up on the exiles, and he cared for those far from home.

d231-letter.title: A letter to the exiles
d231-letter.story: Jeremiah writes a letter to the exiles in Babylon. He tells them to build houses and live in them, plant gardens and eat what they produce, marry and have children, and to seek the welfare of the city where they are, because in its welfare they will find theirs. He says that after seventy years the Lord will bring them back. In Jeremiah 29:11 God says, "I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a future and a hope."
d231-letter.why: This letter was written to people who felt stuck, and it says that they can still plant gardens and care for where they are.

d232-clay_jar.title: The field at Anathoth
d232-clay_jar.story: With Babylon besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah locked in the court of the guard, God tells him that his cousin will offer to sell him a field at Anathoth. Jeremiah buys it, weighs out the silver, signs the deed in front of witnesses, and has Baruch put the deeds in a clay jar to last a long time. It is a sign that houses and fields will again be bought in this land. Earlier, in chapter 31, God promised a new covenant written on their hearts.
d232-clay_jar.why: Buying a field in a city under siege is an act of hope, and it shows faith can look like planning for the future.

d233-scroll.title: The scroll burned
d233-scroll.story: Jehudi reads Jeremiah's scroll aloud to King Jehoiakim, and as he reads, the king cuts off a few columns at a time with a knife and throws them into the fire in the brazier until the whole scroll is burned. Jeremiah is not there, because he and Baruch have been told to hide. God tells Jeremiah to take another scroll and write all the same words again, and Baruch writes them down, and many similar words are added. In chapter 33 God also promises healing and restoration.
d233-scroll.why: A king could burn the scroll, but the words were written again, which suggests the message was not simply paper.

d234-well.title: Jeremiah in the cistern
d234-well.story: As Babylon presses on Jerusalem, Jeremiah is accused of deserting to the enemy, and he is beaten and put in prison. Officials later throw him into a cistern with no water and only mud at the bottom, where he sinks in. Ebed-melech, a Cushite official in the king's house, speaks to the king and gets permission to pull him out with ropes, putting rags under his arms. When the city falls in chapter 39, the Lord promises to save Ebed-melech because he trusted in him.
d234-well.why: One person who spoke up at the right time saved Jeremiah's life, so it is worth speaking when someone is in trouble.

d235-caravan.title: The flight to Egypt
d235-caravan.story: After Jerusalem fell, Babylon set Gedaliah over the people who were left, but he is murdered by Ishmael. Afraid of what Babylon will do, the people ask Jeremiah to pray and promise to obey whatever the Lord says. He tells them to stay in the land, but they say he is lying and go down to Egypt anyway, taking Jeremiah and Baruch with them. In Egypt, Jeremiah continues to warn them, and they keep making offerings to other gods.
d235-caravan.why: The people asked for guidance and then ignored it when they didn't like the answer, a reminder to listen when it is hard.

d236-battle_camp.title: Egypt defeated at Carchemish
d236-battle_camp.story: Jeremiah 46 begins a long set of messages about foreign nations. First is Egypt, whose army is defeated at Carchemish by the river Euphrates, and its soldiers stumble over one another and fall. Chapters 47 and 48 then speak of the Philistines and of Moab, which had trusted in its wealth and its fortresses. Even here there is some mercy: the Lord says he will restore the fortunes of Moab in days to come, and in chapter 46 he tells Jacob, "Do not fear," and promises he will not make an end of him.
d236-battle_camp.why: God is pictured as the Lord of all nations, so no empire is beyond his notice, and no people is beyond his mercy.

d237-ruins.title: Babylon will fall
d237-ruins.story: Jeremiah 49 speaks about Ammon, Edom, Damascus and Elam, warning that each one's pride and security will not last. Then chapter 50 turns to Babylon, the empire that had overpowered everyone else. It is told it will be taken, its idols shamed, and its people will flee. Meanwhile God says that the people of Israel and Judah will come weeping to seek the Lord, and ask the way to Zion with their faces turned toward it.
d237-ruins.why: Babylon looked unbeatable, but these chapters say that no empire stays on top forever.

d238-treasury.title: The temple vessels taken
d238-treasury.story: Jeremiah 51 describes Babylon as a golden cup in the Lord's hand, which made the whole earth drunk, and says that suddenly Babylon has fallen. Chapter 52 retells the final days of Jerusalem: after a long siege, the city wall was broken through, King Zedekiah was captured and blinded, the temple was burned, and its bronze pillars and bowls were broken up and carried off to Babylon. The book ends with a small spark of hope: King Jehoiachin is released from prison in Babylon and given a seat at the king's table.
d238-treasury.why: The story ends with a small act of kindness that suggests the line of David had not been forgotten.

d239-sun_moon.title: New every morning
d239-sun_moon.story: Lamentations is a set of poems mourning Jerusalem after its fall. It begins, "How lonely lies the city, once so full of people!" and describes weeping through the night with no one to comfort her. In chapter 3 the poet speaks of pain and darkness, and then says, "They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!" The poet says, "The LORD is my portion," and then, "therefore I will hope in Him."
d239-sun_moon.why: Hope can show up in the middle of grief, quietly, and each morning offers mercy that was not used up the day before.

d240-ruins.title: Restore us
d240-ruins.story: Lamentations 4 describes how the gold has lost its shine, and the precious people of Zion are treated like clay jars, and the children beg for bread. Chapter 5 is a prayer of the people: "Remember, O LORD, what has happened to us. Look and see our disgrace!" They say that their inheritance has been turned over to strangers and that their joy has ceased. Near its close comes the cry, "Restore us to Yourself, O LORD, so we may return; renew our days as of old."
d240-ruins.why: The book ends with a prayer rather than an answer, and the prayer is simply to be brought back.

d241-whirlwind.title: The vision by the Chebar
d241-whirlwind.story: Ezekiel was a priest among the exiles by the river Kebar in Babylon. The heavens opened and he saw a whirlwind coming from the north, a great cloud flashing with fire, and four living creatures, each with four faces and four wings, beside wheels within wheels. Above them was a throne and a figure like a man, with light around him like a rainbow, and Ezekiel fell on his face. A voice told him to stand and sent him to a rebellious people, and he ate a scroll that tasted sweet as honey.
d241-whirlwind.why: God appeared to Ezekiel by a river in a foreign land, so God's presence was not confined to Jerusalem.

d242-temple.title: Abominations in the temple
d242-temple.story: Ezekiel acts out signs, shaving his head and beard and dividing the hair, to show what is coming on Jerusalem. In chapter 8, the Spirit lifts him by a lock of his hair and takes him in visions to the temple in Jerusalem. There he sees the elders offering incense to images painted on the walls, women weeping for a foreign god, and men with their backs to the temple bowing to the sun. The Lord says he must now act.
d242-temple.why: The vision shows how worship can drift from God while the building still stands, and why God cared about hearts and not just ritual.

d243-cloud_mount.title: The glory leaves the temple
d243-cloud_mount.story: Ezekiel sees a man in linen go through Jerusalem and put a mark on the foreheads of those who grieve over the evil in the city. Then he sees the glory of the Lord rise from the cherubim, move to the threshold of the temple, then to the east gate, and finally rise from the city and stand on the mountain east of it. In chapter 11 God promises to give the people a new spirit, and to take out their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh.
d243-cloud_mount.why: Even as the glory leaves, it ends with a promise of a new heart, which means God was not finished with his people.

d244-vine.title: The useless vine
d244-vine.story: Ezekiel 15 asks what use the wood of a vine is: you cannot make anything from it, not even a peg to hang things on, and it is only fit to burn. God says this is how Jerusalem is. In chapter 16 he tells the story of a baby left in a field whom he found, washed and cared for, and who grew up and then abandoned him. Even so, God says he will remember his covenant, and make an everlasting covenant with her.
d244-vine.why: These stories are painful, but they end by saying that God's love is faithful even when the people are not.

d245-cedar.title: Eagles and the cedar
d245-cedar.story: Ezekiel tells a riddle about a great eagle that takes the top shoot of a cedar to a land of merchants. Another eagle appears and the vine bends toward it, a picture of the kings of Judah and their shifting alliances. In chapter 18 the people say the fathers ate sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge. God says that is no longer a proverb in Israel: each person answers for their own life, and he takes no pleasure in anyone's death but wants them to turn and live.
d245-cedar.why: Each person is responsible for their own choices, and the way back is always open if you turn.

d246-signpost.title: The sword at the fork in the road
d246-signpost.story: Ezekiel is told to set his face against Jerusalem and speak about a sword drawn from its sheath, sharpened and polished. In chapter 21 the king of Babylon stands at a fork in the road, where the road splits to Rabbah of the Ammonites and to Jerusalem in Judah. He shakes the arrows, consults the household gods and looks at the liver, and the omen points to Jerusalem. The chapter also says that the crown will be removed until the one to whom it rightly belongs comes.
d246-signpost.why: The passage is hard reading, but it says that even a king's choices are in God's hands.

d247-city_wall.title: A gap in the wall
d247-city_wall.story: Ezekiel 22 calls Jerusalem a city of blood, listing how its leaders and people have oppressed the foreigner, the orphan and the widow. God says, "I searched for a man among them to repair the wall and stand in the gap before Me on behalf of the land, so that I should not destroy it. But I found no one." Chapter 23 then tells a story of two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, to picture Samaria and Jerusalem, who both turned to other nations instead of to God.
d247-city_wall.why: God was looking for someone to stand in the gap, and the line makes you ask who in your own place can do that.

d248-ship.title: The ship of Tyre
d248-ship.story: Ezekiel is told to write down the day Babylon laid siege to Jerusalem. Then his wife died, and God told him not to mourn aloud, as a sign to the people about the temple being lost. Chapters 26 and 27 then turn to Tyre, the wealthy trading city on the coast. Tyre is pictured as a splendid ship made of cypress and cedar, trading with many nations, loaded with goods. The poem says that ship will be wrecked in the heart of the seas, and the sailors mourn for it.
d248-ship.why: A great trading city looked unsinkable, but this lament says that wealth cannot save anyone.

d249-pyramids.title: Egypt falls
d249-pyramids.story: Ezekiel 28 speaks to the prince of Tyre, who said, "I am a god," and says he is only a man. Chapters 29 and 30 turn to Pharaoh and Egypt, called a great monster lying in the midst of his streams, who said the Nile was his own. God says he will put hooks in his jaws and drag him out. Egypt will become a waste, and the people will know that he is the Lord. The prophecy also says that Israel will no longer lean on Egypt.
d249-pyramids.why: Rulers can start to think they own the river, and God reminds them they do not.

d250-watchtower.title: The watchman
d250-watchtower.story: God appoints Ezekiel as a watchman for the house of Israel. If the watchman sees the sword coming and blows the trumpet, the people are warned, but if he stays silent, he is accountable. God says, "As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked should turn from their ways and live." Then someone who escaped arrives with news that Jerusalem has fallen. The people listen to Ezekiel as if he were singing love songs, but they do not act on his words.
d250-watchtower.why: A watchman's job is to say what he sees, and that includes the hope that people can still turn.

d251-pasture.title: The shepherds of Israel
d251-pasture.story: Ezekiel 34 speaks against the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves and not the sheep, who have not strengthened the weak or bound up the injured. God says he will search for his sheep himself and rescue them from all the places they were scattered. He will bring them to good pasture, bind up the injured and strengthen the weak, and he will set one shepherd over them, his servant David. In chapter 36 he promises to sprinkle clean water on them and give them a new heart.
d251-pasture.why: Good leadership is shown by how the weakest are treated, and God describes himself as a shepherd who goes looking.

d252-dry_bones.title: The valley of dry bones
