d252-dry_bones.story: The hand of the Lord set Ezekiel down in the middle of a valley full of dry bones. God asked, "Son of man, can these bones come to life?" and Ezekiel answered, "only You know." He prophesied to the bones, and with a rattling they came together, flesh and skin covered them, and then breath entered and they stood up, a great army. God said the bones are the whole house of Israel, who say, "Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished; we are cut off."
d252-dry_bones.why: When hope feels completely gone, this vision says God can bring life where nobody expects it.

d253-temple.title: The vision of the new temple
d253-temple.story: In the twenty-fifth year of the exile, Ezekiel is carried in visions to a very high mountain in Israel, where a man whose appearance is like bronze stands at a gate with a linen cord and a measuring rod. The man measures the gates, courts and walls of a new temple, and tells Ezekiel to look carefully, listen and take it all to heart, so that he can tell the house of Israel what he sees. Chapters 40 to 42 give the measurements in detail.
d253-temple.why: For people far from home, the vision gives a plan for a restored place of worship, and it says God was still thinking about their future.

d254-city_gate.title: The closed gate
d254-city_gate.story: In Ezekiel 43 the glory of the Lord enters the new temple by the gate facing east, the same way it left. The sound is like the sound of many waters, and the land shines with his glory, and Ezekiel falls on his face. The Lord says this is the place of his throne, where he will dwell among the people forever. Chapter 44 says the east gate will stay shut because the Lord has entered by it, and only the prince may sit in it to eat bread before the Lord.
d254-city_gate.why: The glory that left in Ezekiel 10 comes back, which is a picture of God returning to a people he had not abandoned.

d255-rivertree.title: The river from the temple
d255-rivertree.story: Ezekiel sees water flowing from the threshold of the temple toward the east. The man with the measuring line takes him out, and the water is first ankle-deep, then knee-deep, then waist-deep, and then a river that cannot be crossed. It flows down to the Dead Sea and makes the salt water fresh, so that fish live in it, and on its banks grow trees with leaves that never wither and fruit every month. The book ends with a new name for the city: "The Lord is there."
d255-rivertree.why: Life flows outward from God's presence, and wherever the river goes, things come back to life.

d256-furnace.title: The fiery furnace
d256-furnace.story: Daniel and three friends are taken to Babylon to serve the king, and the friends are given new names: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. In chapter 3, King Nebuchadnezzar sets up a gold statue and orders everyone to bow to it when the music plays. The three friends refuse and are thrown into a blazing furnace, saying God can save them, but even if he does not, they will not worship the statue. The king sees a fourth figure walking with them in the fire, and they come out unharmed.
d256-furnace.why: They decided to be faithful whatever the outcome, and the story says they were not alone in the fire.

d257-handwriting.title: The writing on the wall
d257-handwriting.story: King Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great tree cut down, and Daniel tells him it means the king will lose his mind for a time until he acknowledges that the Most High rules. It happens as he said, and when the seven times have passed, the king looks up to heaven, his sanity returns, and he praises God. At a later feast, King Belshazzar drinks from the cups taken from the temple, and fingers of a human hand write on the wall. Daniel reads the words, and that very night Belshazzar is killed and Darius the Mede takes the kingdom.
d257-handwriting.why: Pride is a poor foundation for a throne, and these stories say that the one who gives power can take it back.

d258-lions.title: Daniel in the lions' den
d258-lions.story: Daniel served under King Darius, who planned to put him over the whole kingdom. Jealous officials tricked the king into signing a law that anyone who prayed to anyone but the king for thirty days would be thrown to the lions. Daniel kept praying to God as he always had, three times a day at his open window. Darius was distressed, but the law could not be changed, and Daniel was put in the lions' den with a stone sealed over it. At dawn the king hurried back and found Daniel unharmed, because God had shut the lions' mouths.
d258-lions.why: It shows steady, daily faithfulness holding up under pressure, and it ends with the king honoring God.

d259-scroll.title: Daniel prays for his people
d259-scroll.story: Daniel is reading the scrolls and realizes that the seventy years Jeremiah spoke about are nearly over. He turns to God with prayer and fasting, in sackcloth and ashes, and confesses the sins of his people, saying, "we are not presenting our petitions before You because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion." While he is still praying, the angel Gabriel comes to him. In chapters 10 and 11 a messenger tells him not to be afraid, because his words were heard, and shows him kingdoms rising and falling.
d259-scroll.why: Daniel prays for his whole people and rests his request on God's mercy rather than anyone's merit.

d260-stars.title: Those who shine like stars
d260-stars.story: The book of Daniel ends with a promise that many who sleep in the dust will awake, some to everlasting life, and that the wise will shine like the sky, and those who lead many to righteousness like the stars forever. Daniel is told to go his way until the end. Then the book of Hosea begins. God tells Hosea to marry Gomer, a woman who will be unfaithful, as a picture of how Israel has been unfaithful to God, and God says he will still bring her back.
d260-stars.why: The book of Daniel ends on hope, and Hosea starts a picture of love that does not quit on a person.

d261-whirlwind.title: Sowing the wind
d261-whirlwind.story: Hosea 6 says, "Come, let us return to the LORD. For He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us." But the people's love is like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes away early. God says he desires steadfast love and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. In chapter 8 he says they sow the wind and they shall reap the whirlwind, and in chapter 10 he calls them to sow righteousness, reap steadfast love and break up their unplowed ground.
d261-whirlwind.why: Good intentions fade like morning dew unless they are rooted in real love and daily change.

d262-plagues.title: The locust swarm
d262-plagues.story: Hosea 11 shows God as a parent who loved Israel as a child, taught him to walk and took him up in his arms. He says, "How could I give you up, O Ephraim?" Hosea 14 ends with a call to return. Then Joel begins with a plague of locusts that strips the land bare, and the priests are told to call a fast and gather the people to cry out to the Lord. In chapter 2 the call is, "So rend your hearts and not your garments, and return to the LORD your God," for he is gracious and compassionate.
d262-plagues.why: God is shown as a parent who cannot let go, and the call is to come back with your whole heart.

d263-signpost.title: The valley of decision
d263-signpost.story: Joel 3 describes the nations being gathered in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, and the crowds in the valley of decision, because the day of the Lord is near. It also says the Lord is a refuge for his people and that a fountain will flow from his house. Then the book of Amos begins. Amos was a shepherd from Tekoa, and he speaks about the sins of Israel's neighbors and then of Israel itself, saying they sell the righteous for silver and trample the head of the poor.
d263-signpost.why: Amos was an ordinary shepherd, and the message is that God can send an ordinary person to speak up for the poor.

d264-stream.title: Let justice roll like water
d264-stream.story: Amos speaks to the wealthy women of Samaria who oppress the poor and crush the needy, and to people who keep up their religious festivals while ignoring justice. God says, "I hate, I despise your feasts! I cannot stand the stench of your solemn assemblies." Then he says, "let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream." Chapters 7 and 8 include visions of a plumb line and a basket of summer fruit, and a warning about those who trample the needy.
d264-stream.why: Worship and justice belong together, and God cares more about fairness than about festivals.

d265-fish.title: Jonah and the great fish
d265-fish.story: God told Jonah to go to the city of Nineveh and warn it, but Jonah boarded a ship heading the other way. A great storm came, and Jonah told the sailors to throw him overboard, and the sea grew calm. A great fish swallowed him, and Jonah spent three days and nights inside it, praying, before it spat him out onto dry land. Jonah then went to Nineveh, the people turned from their evil, and God showed them mercy, which made Jonah angry.
d265-fish.why: The book ends with a question about God's compassion for people we might not expect, and it leaves the answer to the reader.

d266-plowshare.title: Swords into plowshares
d266-plowshare.story: Micah 2 and 3 speak against leaders who covet fields and take them, and who turn justice upside down. Micah 4 says that in the latter days the mountain of the Lord's house will be established, and many nations will say, "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord." They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks, and nation shall not lift up sword against nation. Chapter 6 asks what the Lord requires: to do justice, to love kindness and to walk humbly with your God.
d266-plowshare.why: The prophet says to do justice, love kindness and walk humbly, which is a clear and short answer to what God asks.

d267-siege.title: Nineveh besieged
d267-siege.story: Nahum speaks about Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, a city known for its cruelty. He says the Lord is slow to anger and a stronghold in the day of trouble. Nineveh will fall, its gates will open, and its soldiers will flee. Habakkuk complains to God, "How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear?" God answers that he is raising up Babylon, and Habakkuk keeps asking why. He stands at his watchpost to see what God will say, and the answer is that the righteous shall live by his faith.
d267-siege.why: Habakkuk asks God hard questions out loud, and waits for an answer, and this is allowed.

d268-fig_tree.title: Though the fig tree does not blossom
d268-fig_tree.story: Habakkuk 3 is a prayer in the form of a song. He trembles at God's mighty acts, then says, "Though the fig tree does not bud and no fruit is on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food," and ends, "yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation!" He says God makes his feet like the feet of a deer. Zephaniah 1 to 3 then warns of the day of the Lord and ends with a promise that God will rejoice over his people with singing.
d268-fig_tree.why: It is a decision to trust and be glad even when nothing is going well.

d269-temple.title: Consider your ways
d269-temple.story: Haggai speaks to the people who returned from exile, who had been busy building their own houses while the Lord's house lay in ruins. He says, "Consider carefully your ways," because they sow much and harvest little. Governor Zerubbabel and the high priest Joshua and the people obey and begin building, and the Lord says, "I am with you." In Zechariah 1 to 3, the prophet has night visions of horsemen, and of Joshua the high priest in dirty clothes who is given clean ones.
d269-temple.why: Haggai asks the people to look honestly at their priorities, and the answer is simple: start building.

d270-lampstand.title: The golden lampstand
d270-lampstand.story: Zechariah sees a lampstand of gold with a bowl on top and seven lamps, and two olive trees beside it that keep it supplied with oil. An angel tells him the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the Lord of hosts." The prophet is also told not to despise the day of small things. Later chapters include visions of a flying scroll, and chapter 9 promises a king who comes humbly, and speaks peace to the nations.
d270-lampstand.why: Big things often start small, and the strength to do them comes from God and not from force.

d270-entry.title: The golden lampstand
d270-entry.story: Zechariah sees a lampstand of gold with a bowl on top and seven lamps, and two olive trees beside it that keep it supplied with oil. An angel tells him the word of the Lord to Zerubbabel: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the Lord of hosts." The prophet is also told not to despise the day of small things. Later chapters include visions of a flying scroll, and chapter 9 promises a king who comes humbly, and speaks peace to the nations.
d270-entry.why: Big things often start small, and the strength to do them comes from God and not from force.

d271-potter.title: King over all the earth
d271-potter.story: In Zechariah 11 the prophet plays the part of a shepherd, and the people pay him thirty pieces of silver as his wages, which he throws to the potter in the house of the Lord. Chapter 12 says the people will look on the one they have pierced and mourn for him, and chapter 13 says, "Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered." Chapter 14 pictures the Lord as king over all the earth. Malachi 1 opens with God saying, "I have loved you."
d271-potter.why: The Gospels later recall these lines about a rejected shepherd, and Malachi opens with the simplest message of all: God loves his people.

d272-stars.title: The star over Bethlehem
d272-stars.story: After Jesus was born in Bethlehem, wise men from the east came to Jerusalem asking where the newborn king of the Jews was, because they had seen his star rise. King Herod was troubled, and the priests told him the prophets pointed to Bethlehem. The star went ahead of the wise men until it stopped over the place where the child was. They knelt and worshipped him and gave gifts of gold, frankincense and myrrh, then went home another way after a warning in a dream not to return to Herod.
d272-stars.why: People from far away come to honor the child, a first sign in Matthew that this story is for everyone.

d273-baptism.title: Baptism in the Jordan
d273-baptism.story: John the Baptist was preaching in the wilderness near the Jordan, calling people to turn from their sins and baptizing those who did. Jesus came from Galilee to be baptized by him, and John at first objected, saying he needed to be baptized by Jesus instead. Jesus said it was right to do this, and John agreed. As Jesus came up out of the water, the heavens opened, the Spirit of God came down like a dove, and a voice from heaven said this was his beloved Son.
d273-baptism.why: It marks the start of Jesus' public work and describes God's approval of him.

d273-nets.title: Nets at the lake
d273-nets.story: Walking beside the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw two brothers, Simon called Peter and Andrew, casting a net into the lake, because they were fishermen. He told them to follow him and said he would make them fish for people. They left their nets at once and followed him. A little farther on he called two more brothers, James and John, who were mending nets in a boat with their father, and they also left and followed.
d273-nets.why: It shows the first followers answering a simple invitation by leaving ordinary work behind.

d274-sermon.title: The sermon on the mountain
d274-sermon.story: Jesus went up on a mountainside, sat down, and began to teach his disciples while a crowd listened. He started with blessings for the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the gentle, those who hunger for what is right, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers and those who are persecuted. He told his listeners that they were salt and light for the world, and he spoke about love for enemies. The teaching continues through chapters 6 and 7, with guidance on prayer and on building a life on his words.
d274-sermon.why: Often called the Sermon on the Mount, it is the best-known summary of how Jesus calls his followers to live.

d274-boat.title: Boat in the storm
d274-boat.story: Jesus got into a boat with his disciples to cross the Sea of Galilee. A violent storm came up, so that the waves swept over the boat, while Jesus was asleep. The frightened disciples woke him and said they were about to die. He asked why they were afraid, then got up and spoke to the wind and the waves, and everything became completely calm. The disciples were amazed and asked what kind of man even the winds and the sea obey.
d274-boat.why: The disciples' question is one the Gospel invites every reader to think about and answer.

d275-treasury.title: The call of Matthew
d275-treasury.story: Matthew chapter 9 tells how Jesus passed a tax collector named Matthew sitting at his booth and said, "Follow me." Matthew got up and followed him, then Jesus ate at his house with other tax collectors and sinners. When people asked why, Jesus said it is the sick who need a doctor, not the healthy. In chapter 10 he chose twelve apostles by name and sent them out to the towns of Israel to announce that the kingdom of heaven was near, to heal the sick and to travel with little.
d275-treasury.why: Jesus invited a person others had written off to walk with him, which says no one is too far gone to be called.

d276-harvest.title: Grain plucked on the Sabbath
d276-harvest.story: In Matthew 11 Jesus invites everyone who is tired and carrying heavy loads to come to him and find rest, saying his yoke is easy and his burden light. Soon after, on the Sabbath, his disciples were hungry and picked heads of grain as they walked through the fields. Some Pharisees objected that this was against the law, and Jesus reminded them how David once ate the consecrated bread in the house of God when he was hungry. He told them God desires mercy, not sacrifice, and that the Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.
d276-harvest.why: Jesus offers rest to anyone who is worn out, and he puts mercy ahead of rule keeping.

d277-sower.title: The sower
d277-sower.story: Jesus sat by the lake, and because the crowd was so large he taught from a boat. He told stories, called parables, about everyday things. In the best known, a farmer scatters seed that falls on the path, on rocky ground, among thorns and on good soil, and only the good soil produces a crop. Jesus later explained that the seed is the message of the kingdom and the soils are the ways people receive it. Other parables in the chapter compare the kingdom to a mustard seed, to yeast, to hidden treasure and to a valuable pearl.
d277-sower.why: Parables invite listeners to think about how they listen and about what is worth giving everything for.

d277-loaves.title: Loaves and fishes
d277-loaves.story: A large crowd had followed Jesus to a quiet place, and by evening they were hungry. The disciples suggested he send the people away to buy food, but Jesus told them to give the people something to eat. They had only five loaves and two fish. Jesus looked up to heaven, gave thanks, broke the loaves and handed them to the disciples to pass around. Everyone ate and was satisfied, and twelve baskets of leftovers were gathered up.
d277-loaves.why: A small offering placed in Jesus' hands becomes more than enough, and the disciples have a part in the giving.

d278-house.title: The faith of the Canaanite woman
d278-house.story: Matthew 15 says Jesus traveled to the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Canaanite woman begged him to heal her daughter, who was suffering badly. At first he did not answer, and his disciples asked him to send her away. She knelt, kept asking for help, and said even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their master's table. Jesus said her faith was great and her daughter was healed from that very hour.
d278-house.why: Her stubborn hope reminds us we can keep asking, and that mercy reaches people beyond the expected circle.

d279-mountain.title: Light on the mountain
d279-mountain.story: Matthew 17 says Jesus took Peter, James and John up a high mountain, where his face shone like the sun and his clothes became white as light. Moses and Elijah appeared and spoke with him. Peter offered to build three shelters, and then a bright cloud covered them and a voice said, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him!" The disciples fell down afraid, but Jesus touched them and told them to get up and not be afraid.
d279-mountain.why: For a moment the disciples saw who Jesus really was, and the voice from the cloud tells us what to do with that: listen.

d280-entry.title: Entry into Jerusalem
d280-entry.story: As Jesus and his disciples came near Jerusalem, he sent two of them to bring a donkey and her colt, and he rode into the city. Many in the crowd spread their cloaks and branches on the road and shouted praise to the Son of David. Matthew says this fulfilled the words of a prophet about a king coming humbly on a donkey. The whole city was stirred and asked who he was, and the crowds said he was the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.
d280-entry.why: It shows what kind of king he is: arriving in humility, not with weapons, only days before the cross.

d281-synagogue.title: Warnings to the teachers
d281-synagogue.story: In Matthew 22 a teacher of the law asked Jesus which commandment is the greatest. Jesus answered that it is to love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul and mind, and the second is like it: love your neighbor as yourself. In chapter 23 he spoke sharply to some of the religious teachers, saying they taught well but did not practice it, and cared more about being noticed than about justice, mercy and faithfulness. He ended with sorrow over Jerusalem, longing to gather its people like a hen gathers her chicks.
d281-synagogue.why: Everything hangs on loving God and loving others, and faith that is only for show misses the point.

d282-ten_lamps.title: Ten lamps waiting
d282-ten_lamps.story: In Matthew 25 Jesus told a story about ten young women waiting with lamps for a bridegroom to arrive at a wedding. Five brought extra oil and five did not. The groom was late, they all fell asleep, and at midnight a cry went up that he was coming. The five without oil ran to buy some and found the door shut when they returned, and Jesus finished by saying, "Keep watch."
d282-ten_lamps.why: The story is a gentle nudge to be ready and to live attentively, not to wait until the last minute.

d283-supper.title: The last supper
d283-supper.story: On the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, Jesus ate the Passover meal with his twelve disciples in Jerusalem. He told them that one of them would betray him. During the meal he took bread, gave thanks, broke it and gave it to them, saying it was his body. Then he took a cup and said it was his blood, poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. They sang a hymn and went out to the Mount of Olives.
d283-supper.why: Many churches remember this meal in communion, each in their own way, and see in it Jesus giving himself for others.

d284-cross.title: The cross and the empty tomb
d284-cross.story: Jesus was handed over to Pilate, who, under pressure from the crowd, gave the order for him to be crucified. Soldiers mocked him and led him out to a place called Golgotha, where he was crucified between two criminals. Darkness covered the land for three hours, and at about the ninth hour Jesus cried out and gave up his spirit. At that moment the curtain of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom, and a Roman centurion said that truly this was the Son of God. Joseph of Arimathea then laid his body in a new tomb.
d284-cross.why: Christians read the cross as the center of the story, where Jesus gives his life for others.

d284-tomb.title: The stone rolled away
d284-tomb.story: After the Sabbath, at dawn on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary went to look at the tomb. There was an earthquake, and an angel rolled back the stone and told the women that Jesus was not there, because he had risen, as he had said. The angel sent them to tell the disciples, and on the way Jesus met them and greeted them. Later, on a mountain in Galilee, he told his disciples to go and make disciples of all nations, and promised to be with them always.
d284-tomb.why: The resurrection is the hope on which Christian faith rests: death is not the last word.

d285-roof_hole.title: The roof opened for a friend
d285-roof_hole.story: Mark 2 tells of Jesus teaching in a house so crowded that no one could get near the door. Four men carrying their paralyzed friend on a mat could not get through, so they dug an opening in the roof and lowered him down in front of Jesus. Seeing their faith, Jesus told the man his sins were forgiven, and then said, "Get up, pick up your mat, and go home." The man stood and walked out in front of everyone, and the crowd was amazed.
d285-roof_hole.why: The man was carried by friends who refused to give up, a picture of how others can bring us to help when we cannot go ourselves.

d286-boat.title: Calm on the lake
d286-boat.story: In Mark 4 Jesus was asleep in a boat when a fierce storm came up on the lake and waves began filling the boat. His frightened disciples woke him, and he told the wind and waves to be still, and there was a great calm. On the far shore in chapter 5, a man who lived among the tombs, tormented and unable to be restrained, met Jesus. Jesus freed him, and the man was later found sitting dressed and calm, and went through the Decapolis telling how much Jesus had done for him.
d286-boat.why: Jesus meets both the storm outside and the turmoil inside, and in each case brings calm.

d287-loaves.title: Five thousand fed
d287-loaves.story: Mark 6 says a huge crowd followed Jesus to a quiet place, and by evening they had nothing to eat. His disciples had only five loaves and two fish. Jesus had the people sit in groups on the grass, gave thanks, broke the bread and gave it to the disciples to hand out. Everyone ate until they were full, and the disciples gathered twelve baskets of leftovers.
d287-loaves.why: A small offering placed in Jesus' hands turned out to be enough, and more than enough.

d288-mountain.title: Seven loaves and a mountain of light
d288-mountain.story: In Mark 8 another large crowd had been with Jesus for three days with nothing left to eat, and he fed about four thousand people with seven loaves and a few small fish. Later, at Bethsaida, he healed a blind man in two touches until the man could see everything clearly. In chapter 9 Jesus led Peter, James and John up a high mountain, where his clothes became dazzling white and a voice from a cloud said, "This is my beloved Son. Listen to him!"
d288-mountain.why: Jesus cares about hunger, sight and the bigger picture, and the voice on the mountain points us back to listening to him.

d289-signpost.title: Bartimaeus by the road
d289-signpost.story: Mark 10 says that as Jesus left Jericho, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus sat by the road and called out, "Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!" Many people told him to be quiet, but he shouted even louder. Jesus stopped and called him over, and Bartimaeus threw off his cloak and came. When Jesus asked what he wanted, he said he wanted to see, and Jesus told him his faith had healed him. He could see at once and followed Jesus along the road.
d289-signpost.why: Bartimaeus would not be hushed, and Jesus stopped for him, a sign that no one's cry is too small to be heard.

d290-treasury.title: The widow's small coins
d290-treasury.story: In Mark 12 Jesus sat in the temple watching people put money into the offering box. Many rich people put in large amounts, and then a poor widow dropped in two small copper coins. Jesus called his disciples over and said she had put in more than all the others, because they gave from what they had to spare and she gave everything she had to live on.
d290-treasury.why: Jesus measures a gift by the heart behind it, not the size of the amount.

d291-perfume_jar.title: Perfume poured out
d291-perfume_jar.story: Mark 14 says that two days before the Passover, Jesus was at a dinner in Bethany when a woman came in with an alabaster jar of very costly perfume. She broke it open and poured it over his head. Some of the guests were upset and said the money should have gone to the poor, but Jesus told them to leave her alone, saying she had done a beautiful thing and had prepared his body for burial ahead of time. He added that wherever the good news was told, what she had done would be remembered.
d291-perfume_jar.why: Her generous love was noticed and honored by Jesus, even when others thought it wasteful.

d292-cross.title: The cross on the hill
d292-cross.story: In Mark 15 Jesus was brought to Pilate, who handed him over to be crucified, and soldiers led him to a place called Golgotha. He was crucified, and a sign above him read "The King of the Jews." At the sixth hour darkness fell over the land, and at the ninth hour Jesus cried out and died. Joseph of Arimathea asked for his body and laid it in a rock tomb. On Sunday morning in chapter 16, some women came to the tomb and found the stone rolled away and a young man in white telling them Jesus had risen.
d292-cross.why: The story pauses at the darkest moment, and the women's discovery at the tomb is where it turns.

d293-hill_town.title: Promises of two births
d293-hill_town.story: Luke 1 tells of the angel Gabriel visiting Mary in Nazareth, telling her she would have a son named Jesus, and Mary answering, "I am the Lord's servant." She traveled to the hill country to visit her relative Elizabeth, who was also expecting, and Elizabeth's baby moved inside her as Mary arrived. Mary then sang a song praising God for lifting up the lowly. When Elizabeth's son was born, her husband Zechariah wrote that the boy's name is John, and he was able to speak again.
d293-hill_town.why: Two ordinary families were drawn into something bigger, and both, in the end, answered with praise.

d294-shepherds.title: Shepherds near Bethlehem
d294-shepherds.story: On the night Jesus was born, shepherds were out in the fields near Bethlehem, keeping watch over their flocks. An angel appeared to them and the glory of the Lord shone around them, and they were terrified. The angel told them not to be afraid, because a Savior had been born that day, and that they would find the baby wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger. A crowd of angels praised God, and the shepherds hurried to Bethlehem, found Mary, Joseph and the baby, and told everyone what they had heard.
d294-shepherds.why: The news first reaches ordinary working people, something Luke takes care to point out.

d294-manger.title: The child is born
d294-manger.story: Matthew begins with the family line of Jesus, then tells how Mary was found to be expecting a child through the Holy Spirit before she and Joseph were married. Joseph was a just man and planned to end the engagement quietly. An angel came to him in a dream and told him to take Mary as his wife and to name the child Jesus. Matthew connects this with the words of a prophet, that a virgin would have a son called Immanuel, which means God with us. The manger itself appears in Luke's account of the birth.
d294-manger.why: Matthew presents the birth as the beginning of God with us, a promise carried by an ordinary family.

d295-nets.title: A catch beyond measure
d295-nets.story: In Luke 4 Jesus spent forty days in the wilderness, where the devil tested him, and Jesus answered each time with words from Scripture. Later, in chapter 5, he was teaching by Lake Gennesaret and asked Simon to push his boat out a little from shore. After teaching, he told Simon to let down the nets for a catch, and though Simon had fished all night and caught nothing, he did it. The nets nearly broke from so many fish, and Simon fell at Jesus' knees, and Jesus told him not to be afraid, because from now on he would catch people.
d295-nets.why: Jesus meets people in their ordinary work, and he says "do not be afraid" at exactly the moment we feel small.

d295-wilderness.title: A catch beyond measure
d295-wilderness.story: In Luke 4 Jesus spent forty days in the wilderness, where the devil tested him, and Jesus answered each time with words from Scripture. Later, in chapter 5, he was teaching by Lake Gennesaret and asked Simon to push his boat out a little from shore. d296-city_gate.title: The widow's son at Nain
d296-city_gate.story: Luke 7 says that as Jesus came near the gate of the town of Nain, a funeral procession was coming out. The dead man was the only son of a widow, and a large crowd was with her. When Jesus saw her, his heart went out to her, and he told her, "Do not weep." He touched the coffin and told the young man, "I tell you, get up!" The young man sat up and began to talk, and Jesus gave him back to his mother.
d296-city_gate.why: Jesus noticed one grieving woman in a crowd and was moved by her pain.

d297-house.title: Seed on four soils and Jairus' daughter
d297-house.story: In Luke 8 Jesus told a story about a farmer scattering seed: some fell on the path, some on rock, some among thorns, and some on good soil, where it grew and produced a large crop. He explained that the seed is God's word and the soils are the different ways people receive it. Later a synagogue leader named Jairus begged Jesus to come to his twelve-year-old daughter, who was dying. News came that she had died, but Jesus took her by the hand and said, "Child, get up!" and she did.
d297-house.why: The seed story asks what kind of soil we are, and the second story says hope is not finished when things look hopeless.

d298-inn.title: The good Samaritan
d298-inn.story: In Luke 10 an expert in the law asked Jesus who his neighbor was. Jesus told of a man beaten and left half dead on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho. A priest and then a Levite saw him and passed by on the other side, but a Samaritan stopped, bandaged his wounds, put him on his own animal and took him to an inn. The Samaritan paid the innkeeper and promised to repay any extra cost. Jesus asked which of the three was a neighbor, and then told the man, "Go and do likewise."
d298-inn.why: Being a neighbor means showing mercy to whoever is in need, whoever they are.

d299-lilies.title: Consider the lilies
d299-lilies.story: Luke 11 says Jesus' disciples asked him to teach them to pray, and he gave them the prayer that begins "Father, hallowed be your name," and encouraged them to keep asking, seeking and knocking. In chapter 12 he told his disciples not to worry about life, what to eat or what to wear. He pointed to the ravens, which neither sow nor reap but are fed, and to the lilies, which are dressed more beautifully than King Solomon. He said that if God cares for these, he will care for them too.
d299-lilies.why: Worry is not shamed here, it is met with a picture of a God who notices birds and flowers and notices you.

d300-mustard.title: The mustard seed
d300-mustard.story: In Luke 13 Jesus said the kingdom of God is like a mustard seed that someone plants in a garden. It grows into a tree large enough for the birds to nest in its branches. He also compared it to yeast that a woman mixes into a large amount of flour until it works through the whole batch. In chapter 14 he told of a great banquet where the invited guests made excuses, so the host sent his servant to bring in the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame.
d300-mustard.why: Small beginnings can grow into something large, and the invitation to the table is open to people who are often left out.

d300-table.title: The mustard seed
d300-table.story: In Luke 13 Jesus said the kingdom of God is like a mustard seed that someone plants in a garden. It grows into a tree large enough for the birds to nest in its branches. d301-prodigal.title: The father runs to his son
d301-prodigal.story: Jesus told a story about a father with two sons. The younger son asked for his share of the inheritance, left for a distant country and spent it all, and ended up hungry, feeding pigs. He decided to go home and ask to be taken on as a servant. While he was still far off, his father saw him, ran to him, embraced him and held a feast. The older son, who had stayed home, was angry, and the father went out to plead with him as well.
d301-prodigal.why: It pictures forgiveness as being met on the road before the apology is finished, and it leaves open whether the older brother comes in.

d302-sycamore.title: Zacchaeus in the sycamore
d302-sycamore.story: Luke 19 says Jesus was passing through Jericho, where a chief tax collector named Zacchaeus lived. Zacchaeus was short and could not see over the crowd, so he ran ahead and climbed a sycamore tree. When Jesus reached the spot he looked up and said, "Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today." Zacchaeus welcomed him gladly, and promised to give half of what he owned to the poor and to repay anyone he had cheated four times over.
d302-sycamore.why: Jesus went to the house of a man everyone disliked, and being welcomed changed him.

d303-treasury.title: Whose image is on the coin
d303-treasury.story: In Luke 20 the temple leaders and some spies sent to trap Jesus asked him whether it was right to pay taxes to Caesar. Jesus asked for a coin and asked whose picture and name were on it. When they said Caesar's, he told them to give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's. His answer left them with nothing to use against him, and they were silent.
d303-treasury.why: Jesus gave an answer that was calm and wise under pressure, and he pointed past coins to what truly belongs to God.

d304-olive_grove.title: The upper room and the olive grove
d304-olive_grove.story: Luke 22 says Jesus sat down at the Passover meal with his apostles in an upper room. He took bread and gave thanks and broke it, and then a cup, and told them to remember him. Afterward he went out to the Mount of Olives to pray, and he asked his Father, "Not my will, but yours be done." In his anguish an angel strengthened him, and his sweat was like drops of blood. Judas arrived with a crowd and Jesus was arrested.
d304-olive_grove.why: In his hardest hour Jesus prayed honestly, and it shows that praying through fear and trust together is allowed.

d305-tomb.title: The cross and a tomb
d305-tomb.story: Luke 23 says Jesus was brought before Pilate and then Herod, and the crowd shouted for him to be crucified. At a place called the Skull he was crucified between two criminals, and he said, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing." One of the criminals asked Jesus to remember him, and Jesus told him he would be with him in paradise. Jesus then cried out and breathed his last, and Joseph of Arimathea laid his body in a tomb cut in the rock, where no one had been laid before.
d305-tomb.why: Even in suffering, Jesus offered forgiveness and welcome, and the Gospel records his last words with great gentleness.

d306-signpost.title: The road to Emmaus
d306-signpost.story: Luke 24 says that on the Sunday of the resurrection, two followers of Jesus were walking to the village of Emmaus, talking sadly about all that had happened. A stranger joined them and explained from the Scriptures what had been said about the Messiah, but they did not recognize him. At supper he took bread, gave thanks and broke it, and their eyes were opened and they saw it was Jesus. They hurried back to Jerusalem to tell the others. John 1 then begins with the Word who was with God and was God, a light that shines in the darkness.
d306-signpost.why: Their hearts burned as Jesus spoke, and sometimes we only recognize him in hindsight, in the simple things.

d307-cana.title: Water into wine
d307-cana.story: Jesus, his mother and his disciples were guests at a wedding in Cana in Galilee when the wine ran out. The mother of Jesus told him about it and then told the servants to do whatever he said. He had them fill six large stone water jars with water, then draw some out and take it to the master of the feast. It had become wine, and the master remarked that the best had been kept until last. John calls this the first of Jesus' signs, and says his disciples believed in him.
d307-cana.why: John begins the signs at an ordinary celebration, showing Jesus caring about joy in everyday life.

d307-well.title: Water into wine
d307-well.story: Jesus, his mother and his disciples were guests at a wedding in Cana in Galilee when the wine ran out. The mother of Jesus told him about it and then told the servants to do whatever he said. d308-pool.title: The pool of Bethesda
d308-pool.story: John 5 says that in Jerusalem, beside a pool called Bethesda, many sick, blind and lame people lay waiting. Jesus saw a man who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years and asked him, "Do you want to get well?" The man said he had no one to help him into the water. Jesus told him, "Get up, pick up your mat and walk," and he did, though it was the Sabbath and some of the leaders objected.
d308-pool.why: Jesus saw a man who had been forgotten for decades and spoke to him directly.

d309-loaves.title: The bread of life
d309-loaves.story: John 6 says that after Jesus fed a crowd of about five thousand with five loaves and two fish, the people followed him across the lake looking for more. Jesus told them not to work for food that spoils, but for food that lasts. He said, "I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will never hunger." Many people found his teaching hard and left, and Peter said that Jesus had the words of eternal life, so where else could they go? Chapter 7 describes the feast of Tabernacles and the people arguing about who he was.
d309-loaves.why: Jesus offers himself as what we are truly hungry for, even when his words are hard to take in.

d310-lamp.title: Light of the world
d310-lamp.story: In John 8 Jesus was teaching in the temple courts, near the treasury. He said, "I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life." Earlier in the chapter, some teachers brought a woman caught in a serious wrong and asked whether she should be punished. Jesus said the one without sin should throw the first stone, and one by one they left. He told her he did not condemn her and to go and sin no more.
d310-lamp.why: The light Jesus brings shows what is real, but it comes with mercy, not condemnation.

d311-pasture.title: The good shepherd
d311-pasture.story: John 9 tells how Jesus met a man blind from birth, put mud on his eyes and told him to wash in the pool of Siloam. The man came back able to see, and the leaders questioned him closely. In chapter 10 Jesus said, "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep." He said his sheep know his voice, and that he would give them life to the full.
d311-pasture.why: A shepherd knows each sheep by name, and Jesus says that is how he knows you.

d311-pool.title: The good shepherd
d311-pool.story: John 9 tells how Jesus met a man blind from birth, put mud on his eyes and told him to wash in the pool of Siloam. d312-cave.title: Lazarus, come out
d312-cave.story: John 11 says Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Mary and Martha and a friend of Jesus, was sick and died. When Jesus arrived, he had already been in the tomb four days. Martha said she believed Jesus was the Messiah, Jesus wept, and then he went to the tomb and told them to take away the stone. He called out in a loud voice, "Lazarus, come out!" and the dead man walked out, still wrapped in grave cloths. Many who saw it believed in him.
d312-cave.why: Jesus is not distant from grief, since he wept first and then called Lazarus back.

d313-basin.title: Washing the feet
d313-basin.story: In John 13 Jesus and his disciples were at supper before the Passover. He got up, wrapped a towel around his waist, poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet, the job of a servant. Peter protested at first, and Jesus said that unless he washed him, Peter would have no part with him. Afterward Jesus said, "A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another."
d313-basin.why: Greatness here is shown in humble service, and love is the sign that marks his followers.

d314-vine.title: The true vine
d314-vine.story: In John 15 Jesus told his disciples, "I am the vine and you are the branches." He said that a branch cannot bear fruit unless it stays joined to the vine, and that those who remain in him will bear much fruit. He told them to remain in his love and said he had called them friends. In chapter 16 he warned they would have trouble in the world, but said, "Take courage; I have overcome the world!"
d314-vine.why: Fruit comes from staying connected to Jesus, not from trying harder on our own strength.

d315-cross.title: Arrest in the garden and the cross
d315-cross.story: John 18 says Jesus went with his disciples to a garden across a ravine, where Judas arrived with soldiers and Jesus was arrested. He was taken before the high priest and then to Pilate, who found no basis for a charge, yet handed him over to be crucified. At Golgotha, Jesus looked from the cross to his mother and the disciple he loved and asked the disciple to care for her. He said, "It is finished," and died. Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus laid his body in a new tomb in a garden nearby.
d315-cross.why: Jesus is shown as calm and caring to the last, thinking of his mother even on the cross.

d316-tomb.title: The empty tomb at dawn
d316-tomb.story: John 20 says that early on Sunday, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb and found the stone moved. She stood weeping outside until Jesus, whom she took for the gardener, said her name, and she knew him. That evening he appeared to his disciples, and a week later he appeared to Thomas, who had doubted. In chapter 21 Jesus cooked breakfast for the disciples on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias, and asked Peter three times, "Do you love me?" before telling him to feed his sheep. Acts 1 then describes Jesus rising into the sky and the disciples waiting in Jerusalem.
d316-tomb.why: Jesus said her name and she knew him, a picture of being known personally.

d316-shore.title: The empty tomb at dawn
d316-shore.story: John 20 says that early on Sunday, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb and found the stone moved. That evening he appeared to his disciples, and a week later he appeared to Thomas, who had doubted. d317-pentecost.title: Pentecost
d317-pentecost.story: Jesus' followers were together in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost when a sound like a rushing wind filled the house. What looked like tongues of fire rested on each of them, and they were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages. Visitors from many nations, gathered in the city, heard them talking about the wonders of God in their own languages. Peter stood up and explained what was happening, and about three thousand people were baptized that day.
d317-pentecost.why: The gift crosses language barriers, and it marks the beginning of the church's life and mission.

d317-temple_gate.title: Pentecost
d317-temple_gate.story: Jesus' followers were together in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost when a sound like a rushing wind filled the house. What looked like tongues of fire rested on each of them, and they were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages. Visitors from many nations, gathered in the city, heard them talking about the wonders of God in their own languages. Peter stood up and explained what was happening, and about three thousand people were baptized that day.
