d318-synagogue.title: Boldness before the council
d318-synagogue.story: Acts 4 says Peter and John were arrested after healing a man and preaching, and brought before the Jewish council the next day. They were asked by what power they had done this, and Peter said it was by the name of Jesus. The council saw how bold the two were, as they were ordinary men, and ordered them to stop speaking about Jesus. Peter and John replied that they could not help speaking about what they had seen and heard. In chapter 5 the apostles were put in jail, an angel let them out at night, and they went straight back to the temple to teach.
d318-synagogue.why: They were not trying to be defiant, only faithful to what they believed was true.

d319-chariot.title: Philip and the Ethiopian
d319-chariot.story: Acts 8 says an angel sent Philip to a desert road, where he met an Ethiopian official in charge of the queen's treasury, riding in a chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah. Philip asked if he understood it, and the man said he needed someone to explain it. Philip climbed in and told him the good news about Jesus. When they came to some water, the official asked, "What is there to prevent me from being baptized?" and Philip baptized him. He went on his way rejoicing.
d319-chariot.why: Sharing faith can start with a question and a willingness to sit alongside someone.

d320-damascus.title: Light on the Damascus road
d320-damascus.story: Saul was on his way to Damascus to arrest followers of Jesus when a light from heaven flashed around him and he fell to the ground. A voice asked why he was persecuting him, and when Saul asked who was speaking, the voice said it was Jesus. Saul got up blind and was led into the city, where for three days he did not eat or drink. The Lord sent a disciple named Ananias to him, and Ananias objected, because of what Saul had done to believers, but he went, laid hands on Saul, and Saul could see again and was baptized. He soon began telling people in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.
d320-damascus.why: Saul, later known as Paul, turns from opponent to messenger, an example of a life turned around.

d321-chain.title: Peter freed from prison
d321-chain.story: Acts 12 says King Herod arrested Peter and put him in prison under heavy guard, and the church prayed earnestly for him. The night before his trial, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with chains, when an angel woke him and told him to get up. The chains fell off, the iron gate opened by itself, and Peter walked out into the city. He went to the house where the church was praying, and a servant girl named Rhoda was so overjoyed to hear his voice that she ran back inside without opening the gate.
d321-chain.why: The people praying were amazed their prayer was answered, and the story admits that surprise honestly.

d322-ship.title: Barnabas and Saul sent out
d322-ship.story: Acts 13 says that in the church at Antioch, while the leaders were worshiping and fasting, the Holy Spirit said to set apart Barnabas and Saul for a special work. After more fasting and prayer, the church laid hands on them and sent them off. They sailed to Cyprus and then traveled on to Perga, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, speaking in synagogues and to anyone who would listen. Chapter 14 tells of welcome in some places and opposition in others, and how they returned to Antioch and reported all that God had done.
d322-ship.why: The church sent them with prayer, a reminder that faith is meant to be carried out together.

d323-prison.title: Paul and Silas in prison
d323-prison.story: Acts 16 says Paul and Silas were beaten and thrown into prison in Philippi. Around midnight they were praying and singing hymns while the other prisoners listened, and a sudden earthquake shook the prison doors open. The jailer, afraid, was about to take his own life, but Paul called out that they were all still there. The jailer asked what he must do, and that night he washed their wounds, he and his household were baptized, and he served them a meal. Before this, in chapter 15, the church leaders at Jerusalem met to settle questions about welcoming non-Jewish believers.
d323-prison.why: Singing in a cell is a hard-to-imagine kind of trust, and it changed someone's life that night.

d324-altar.title: Paul in Athens
d324-altar.story: Acts 17 says Paul walked through Athens and was troubled to see the city full of idols. He spoke in the marketplace and then at the Areopagus, where he said he had seen an altar inscribed "To an unknown god" and that he wanted to tell them about the God they were worshiping without knowing. He said God made the world and everything in it and is not far from any of us. Some mocked, some wanted to hear more, and a few believed. Chapters 18 and 19 follow him on to Corinth and Ephesus.
d324-altar.why: Paul began with what his listeners already knew and treated their searching with respect.

d325-shore.title: The farewell on the beach
d325-shore.story: Acts 20 says Paul was on his way to Jerusalem and called the elders of the church at Ephesus to meet him at Miletus. He reminded them how he had served among them with humility, and told them to watch over the flock and care for it. He said he did not know exactly what awaited him in Jerusalem except that hardship was likely, and that they would not see his face again. He knelt with them and prayed, they all wept as they said goodbye, and then they walked him to the ship. In chapter 21, at Tyre, believers and their families knelt on the beach to pray with him before he sailed on.
d325-shore.why: It is a tender goodbye, and a reminder that leaving well matters as much as arriving.

d326-palace.title: Paul before the governor
d326-palace.story: Acts 22 gives the speech Paul made from the steps of the barracks after he was seized in Jerusalem, telling the crowd how he had met Jesus. Later he stood before the Jewish council, and then before the governor Felix in Caesarea. Paul calmly said he had done nothing wrong and that he was on trial for his hope in the resurrection. Felix kept him in custody for two years, hoping for a bribe.
d326-palace.why: Paul told the truth plainly to the governor and did not bend it to buy his own freedom.

d327-shipwreck.title: The storm and the shipwreck
d327-shipwreck.story: Acts 27 says Paul, a prisoner, was put on a ship headed for Rome with other prisoners and a Roman officer named Julius. The weather turned bad, and a fierce wind called the northeaster drove the ship for many days, with no sun or stars in sight. The crew gave up hope, but Paul told them an angel had said that everyone on board would survive, though the ship would be lost. He urged them to eat, and then the ship hit a sandbar and the stern began to break apart in the waves. Everyone on board, 276 people in all, reached land, some swimming and some on planks.
d327-shipwreck.why: In the middle of fear, Paul spoke a calm word and encouraged everyone to keep going.

d327-ship.title: The storm and the shipwreck
d327-ship.story: Acts 27 says Paul, a prisoner, was put on a ship headed for Rome with other prisoners and a Roman officer named Julius. The weather turned bad, and a fierce wind called the northeaster drove the ship for many days, with no sun or stars in sight. The crew gave up hope, but Paul told them an angel had said that everyone on board would survive, though the ship would be lost. He urged them to eat, and then the ship hit a sandbar and the stern began to break apart in the waves. Everyone on board, 276 people in all, reached land, some swimming and some on planks.
d327-ship.why: In the middle of fear, Paul spoke a calm word and encouraged everyone to keep going.

d328-shore.title: Safe ashore on Malta
d328-shore.story: After the shipwreck, the people learned that the island was called Malta. The islanders showed them unusual kindness and lit a fire because of the rain and the cold. Paul gathered a bundle of sticks, and a viper driven out by the heat fastened itself on his hand. The islanders expected him to drop dead, but when he shook it into the fire and was not harmed, they changed their minds and said he was a god. Paul later reached Rome and lived in his own rented house, welcoming everyone who came, and Romans 1 opens his letter to the church there.
d328-shore.why: Strangers warmed a cold, wet crowd with a fire, and Paul kept going and kept telling people about Jesus wherever he landed.

d329-letter.title: A letter to Rome
d329-letter.story: Romans 2 to 4 is part of a letter Paul wrote to the Christians in Rome. He wrote that everyone, Jew and Gentile alike, has fallen short, and that no one is made right with God by keeping the law. He said people are put right with God by faith, as a gift. He pointed to Abraham, who believed God and had it counted to him as righteousness, even before he was circumcised.
d329-letter.why: Paul wanted the Roman believers to know that the way to God is open on the same footing for everyone.

d330-baptism.title: Baptized into a new life
d330-baptism.story: Romans 5 to 8 is a long stretch of Paul's letter to Rome. He wrote that through Jesus we have peace with God and that suffering can build endurance and hope. He wrote that those baptized into Christ Jesus were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, as Christ was raised, they too may walk in newness of life, and said that those in Christ are no longer condemned. The section ends in Romans 8 with the words that nothing, neither death nor life nor anything else in all creation, can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
d330-baptism.why: These chapters are a long line of reassurance, ending with the promise that God's love holds on.

d331-scroll.title: Faith comes by hearing
d331-scroll.story: In Romans 9 and 10 Paul wrote honestly about the great sorrow he felt for his own people, the people of Israel, who had not all accepted Jesus. He said he would even wish himself cut off for their sake. In chapter 10 he wrote that if you declare with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him, you will be saved, and that faith comes from hearing the message. He asked how people can believe without someone to tell them, and quoted Isaiah: "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news."
d331-scroll.why: Paul's grief for his own people shows how much he cared, and it explains why he was so eager to share the message.

d332-olive_grove.title: The olive tree
d332-olive_grove.story: In Romans 11 Paul pictured God's people as an olive tree, with the people of Israel as the natural branches. Some branches had been broken off, and branches from a wild olive, the non-Jewish believers, were grafted in. He warned the new branches not to boast, since they do not support the root, but the root supports them. In chapter 12 he urged believers to offer their bodies as a living sacrifice, not to copy the pattern of the world but to be changed by a renewed mind, and to love one another sincerely.
d332-olive_grove.why: The picture is of one tree with many branches, and the whole is held by a root older than any of us.

d333-signpost.title: Plans to visit Rome
d333-signpost.story: Romans 15 and 16 close Paul's letter to Rome. He told the church he hoped to visit them on his way to Spain, after first taking a gift for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He asked them to pray for him. Chapter 16 is a long list of greetings to people by name, including Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea, Prisca and Aquila, and many others he called friends and fellow workers. First Corinthians 1 then opens with a letter to the church in Corinth, urging unity in the church.
d333-signpost.why: The long list of names is a reminder that Paul's work was carried by many friends, and they are remembered.

d334-vineyard.title: Planting and watering
d334-vineyard.story: In 1 Corinthians 3 Paul addressed a church where people were taking sides, some saying they followed Paul and others Apollos. He asked what Paul and Apollos really were, and answered that they are simply servants. He said, "I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow." He added that neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God, who gives the growth.
d334-vineyard.why: Our part is real but small, and the growth that matters most still belongs to God alone.

d335-race.title: Running for the prize
d335-race.story: In 1 Corinthians 9 Paul used the picture of a race to talk about the way he lived. He said that in a race all the runners run, but only one gets the prize, so run in such a way as to get it. He said athletes train hard for a crown that will not last, but believers aim for one that will. Paul said he does not run aimlessly and that he keeps his body in training so that he does not miss the goal himself.
d335-race.why: A steady, trained, purposeful life beats drifting, and the prize in view helps with the effort.

d336-supper.title: The Lord's supper
d336-supper.story: In 1 Corinthians 11 Paul reminded the church of what he had passed on to them. On the night he was betrayed, Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said it was his body for them, and told them to do this in remembrance of him. In the same way he took the cup and said it was the new covenant in his blood. Paul said every time they eat the bread and drink the cup, they proclaim the Lord's death until he comes, and he urged them to come together to the meal with care and consideration for each other.
d336-supper.why: The meal looks back to the last supper and invites those who share it to be kind to one another.

d337-love.title: Love is patient and kind
d337-love.story: Paul wrote to the church in Corinth, which was divided and proud of its spiritual gifts. In this chapter he says that speaking in angelic tongues, knowing every mystery, or giving everything away means nothing without love. He then describes love as patient and kind, not envious or boastful, not self-seeking and not easily angered. It rejoices in the truth, and it bears and endures all things. He ends by saying that faith, hope and love last, and that love is the greatest of the three.
d337-love.why: It is often read at weddings, yet it was written to a quarreling congregation, so it is about how people treat one another every day.

d338-tomb.title: Raised imperishable
d338-tomb.story: In 1 Corinthians 15 Paul wrote that the message he had received and passed on was that Christ died, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to many people, including Peter, the Twelve and more than five hundred at once. He said that if Christ has not been raised, their faith is useless, but that in fact Christ has been raised, and so those who belong to him will be raised as well. He described the body as sown perishable and raised imperishable. Near the end he wrote, "Where, O death, is your victory?"
d338-tomb.why: Paul's hope is that death is not the last word, and he writes about it with joy.

d339-clay_jar.title: Treasure in jars of clay
d339-clay_jar.story: In 2 Corinthians 4 Paul wrote that people who carry the good news have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the power belongs to God and not to them. He said they are pressed on every side but not crushed, perplexed but not in despair, struck down but not destroyed. He said that although outwardly we are wasting away, inwardly we are being renewed day by day. In chapter 5 he said that we walk by faith, not by sight.
d339-clay_jar.why: Being cracked and fragile is not the end of the story, since the treasure is inside.

d340-firstfruits.title: The cheerful giver
d340-firstfruits.story: In 2 Corinthians 8 and 9 Paul asked the church in Corinth to join in a collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He held up the churches of Macedonia, who gave generously even though they were poor themselves. He told the Corinthians each person should give what they have decided in their heart, not reluctantly or under pressure, because God loves a cheerful giver. He added that whoever sows generously will also reap generously.
d340-firstfruits.why: Giving is meant to come from a willing and cheerful heart, and not from guilt or pressure.

d341-city_wall.title: Lowered in a basket
d341-city_wall.story: In 2 Corinthians 11 Paul listed hardships he had faced: beatings, shipwrecks, danger on the roads, hunger and sleepless nights. He told how in Damascus he was let down in a basket through an opening in the city wall and so escaped. In chapter 12 he spoke of a "thorn in my flesh" that he asked three times to have removed, and that God answered, "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is perfected in weakness." Paul said he would therefore boast in his weaknesses.
d341-city_wall.why: Paul found that being weak and needing help is not a failure, and that God's grace meets us there.

d342-stars.title: Abraham's children by faith
d342-stars.story: Galatians 1 to 4 is a letter Paul wrote to churches in Galatia. He described how he came to follow Jesus and said the message he preached came by revelation from Jesus himself. He argued that people are made right with God by faith in Christ and not by following the law, and used Abraham as an example, who believed God and had it counted to him as righteousness. He wrote that those who have faith are children of Abraham, and that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for all are one.
d342-stars.why: Paul's point is that the family of faith is open to everyone on the same terms, and no one is shut out by birth or status.

d343-fig_tree.title: The fruit of the Spirit
d343-fig_tree.story: In Galatians 5 Paul urged the believers to live by the Spirit and not follow the desires of the flesh. He listed the fruit of the Spirit as love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control, and said there is no law against such things. In chapter 6 he told them to carry each other's burdens and not to grow weary of doing good. Ephesians 1 then begins another letter, praising God for blessing his people and praying that they would know the hope to which he has called them.
d343-fig_tree.why: Fruit grows slowly and naturally, and the list reads like a portrait of a good life.

d344-lamp.title: Saved by grace, walking in the light
d344-lamp.story: In Ephesians 2 Paul wrote that people were once dead in their wrongdoing, but that God, who is rich in mercy, made them alive in Christ. He said, "For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast." He said that Jews and non-Jews are now one people in Christ. In chapters 4 and 5 he urged believers to live as children of light, to be kind and forgiving to one another, and to love as Christ loved.
d344-lamp.why: The gift comes first and the changed life follows, and not the other way round.

d345-armor.title: The armor of God
d345-armor.story: In Ephesians 6 Paul told the believers to be strong in the Lord and to put on the full armor of God. He described a belt of truth, a breastplate of righteousness, shoes ready with the good news of peace, a shield of faith, a helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. He added that they should pray at all times. In Philippians 1 and 2, written from prison, he said that to live is Christ, urged humility and unity, and described how Jesus humbled himself and was then lifted up.
d345-armor.why: The armor is made of truth, peace and faith, which are the things that hold up when life is hard.

d346-race.title: Pressing toward the goal
d346-race.story: In Philippians 3 Paul said that he counted everything he had once been proud of as loss compared to knowing Christ. He said that he had not yet reached the goal, but that he was forgetting what lay behind and pressing on toward what lay ahead. In chapter 4 he wrote, "Rejoice in the Lord always," told them not to be anxious but to pray about everything with thanks, and promised that the peace of God would guard their hearts. Colossians 1 then begins another letter, praising Christ as the image of the invisible God.
d346-race.why: Paul writes from prison about joy, which shows how it can grow in the hardest places.

d347-white_robes.title: Put on a new self
d347-white_robes.story: In Colossians 3 Paul told the believers to set their minds on things above and to take off old habits like anger, slander and greed. He said to put on a new self, a set of clean clothes, made of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. He told them to forgive as the Lord forgave them, and above all to put on love, which binds everything together. He added that whatever they do, they should do it in the name of Jesus with thanks. First Thessalonians 1 then opens with Paul praising the church there for their faith, love and hope.
d347-white_robes.why: Change is described as getting dressed, and a choice to put on kindness each morning.

d348-shofar.title: The trumpet call
d348-shofar.story: In 1 Thessalonians 4 Paul wrote to believers who were grieving for friends who had died. He did not want them to grieve without hope, and told them that those who have died in Christ are not forgotten. He wrote that the Lord himself will come down with a loud command and the sound of a trumpet, and that all who belong to him will be with him forever. In chapter 5 he told them to encourage each other, to be alert and ready, and to hold on to what is good.
d348-shofar.why: Paul wrote these words to comfort people who were grieving, and he meant them as hope.

d349-letter.title: Letters to Timothy
d349-letter.story: In 2 Thessalonians 2 and 3 Paul encouraged the church to stand firm and to keep working steadily as they waited. Then in 1 Timothy 1 to 3 he wrote to Timothy, a younger coworker whom he called his true child in the faith, who was caring for the church at Ephesus. He asked that prayers be made for everyone, including kings and those in authority, and described the kind of character that leaders in the church should have: respected, self-controlled, gentle and hospitable.
d349-letter.why: The letters are the advice of an older friend to a younger one, with a lot of care in it.

d350-altar.title: Fan into flame
d350-altar.story: In 1 Timothy 6 Paul told Timothy to flee the love of money, which is a root of all kinds of evil, and instead to pursue righteousness, faith, love and gentleness, and to fight the good fight of faith. In 2 Timothy 1, Paul wrote from prison, remembering Timothy's tears and the faith that had first lived in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. He told Timothy to fan into flame the gift of God, because God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power, love and self-control.
d350-altar.why: A small flame can be kept alive or let fade, and Paul wants Timothy to tend his.

d351-scroll.title: All Scripture is useful
d351-scroll.story: In 2 Timothy 2 Paul urged Timothy to be strong, to endure hardship like a good soldier and to be an unashamed worker who handles the word of truth well. In chapter 3 he wrote that all Scripture is breathed out by God and is useful for teaching, correcting and training in righteousness, so that the person of God may be fully equipped. In chapter 4 Paul wrote that he had fought the good fight, finished the race and kept the faith. Titus 1 and 2 then give advice to Titus on leading the church on the island of Crete.
d351-scroll.why: Scripture is described as practical, a tool for living well, and not just a book to admire.

d352-chain.title: The appeal for Onesimus
d352-chain.story: Titus 3 finishes Paul's short letter to Titus, urging believers to be ready to do good, to be gentle, and to show humility toward everyone. The short letter to Philemon is a personal appeal. Onesimus, Philemon's slave, had been separated from him for a while and had come to faith through Paul while Paul was in chains. Paul sent him back with the letter and asked Philemon to welcome him "no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother." Hebrews 1 and 2 then begin a letter showing that Jesus is greater than the angels.
d352-chain.why: Paul asks for mercy for a man with no power, and asks Philemon to see him as a brother.

d353-anchor.title: The anchor of hope
d353-anchor.story: Hebrews 3 to 7 is part of a letter urging believers to hold on and not give up. The writer encouraged them to hold firm to their confidence, to enter God's rest, and to draw near with confidence to the throne of grace to find mercy. In chapter 6 he wrote that God's promise is a hope we have as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. He described Jesus as a high priest who understands our weaknesses and who always lives to speak for us.
d353-anchor.why: An anchor does not remove the storm, but it keeps the ship from drifting away.

d354-tabernacle.title: The ark and the tent
d354-tabernacle.story: Hebrews 8 to 10 looks back to the tent of meeting, the tabernacle, that Moses built in the wilderness, with its ark of the covenant, its lampstand and its table. The writer explained that the old sacrifices had to be repeated again and again, and that Jesus offered himself once. He wrote that God promised a new covenant with his law written on people's hearts. He urged the readers to draw near with a sincere heart, to hold on to hope, and to keep meeting together to encourage each other.
d354-tabernacle.why: The tent was a picture pointing toward something, and the letter says that something has now come.

d355-faith.title: The hall of faith
d355-faith.story: This chapter describes faith as trusting in what we hope for, even though we cannot see it. It then walks through the Old Testament, naming people who acted on God's promises, among them Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham and Sarah, Moses and Rahab. Some saw great victories and others suffered, and the chapter says they did not receive everything promised in their own lifetimes. It leads into the next chapter's call to run the race with perseverance.
d355-faith.why: It gives a long line of ordinary, flawed people who trusted God, which makes faith feel shared and handed down.

d356-ship.title: Taming the tongue
d356-ship.story: James 1 to 3 is a short, practical letter. James said to count it all joy when you face trials, because testing builds endurance, and to be quick to listen and slow to speak. In chapter 3 he wrote that the tongue is small, like the rudder that steers a great ship or the bit that guides a horse, but it can do great harm like a spark that sets a forest on fire. He said praise and cursing should not come from the same mouth, and that wisdom from above is pure, peaceable and gentle.
d356-ship.why: Words steer more than we think, which makes it worth choosing them with care.

d357-cornerstone.title: A living stone
d357-cornerstone.story: In James 5 the writer urged believers to be patient, like a farmer who waits for the autumn and spring rains, and to pray for one another. First Peter 1 and 2 are written to scattered believers who were facing hardship. Peter told them they had been given new birth into a living hope. In chapter 2 he called Jesus the living stone, rejected by people but chosen by God, and said that believers are like living stones being built into a spiritual house.
d357-cornerstone.why: You are not just a spectator but one of the stones in a living building.

d357-harvest.title: A living stone
d357-harvest.story: In James 5 the writer urged believers to be patient, like a farmer who waits for the autumn and spring rains, and to pray for one another. First Peter 1 and 2 are written to scattered believers who were facing hardship. Peter told them they had been given new birth into a living hope. In chapter 2 he called Jesus the living stone, rejected by people but chosen by God, and said that believers are like living stones being built into a spiritual house.
d357-harvest.why: You are not just a spectator but one of the stones in a living building.

d358-pasture.title: Shepherds of the flock
d358-pasture.story: In 1 Peter 5 Peter wrote to the elders of the church, as a fellow elder himself and a witness of Christ's suffering. He told them to be shepherds of God's flock, serving not because they must but because they are willing, not for money but eagerly, and not lording it over others but being examples. He told the younger people to be humble toward their elders, and everyone to cast all their anxiety on God because he cares for them. In 2 Peter 1 and 2 he urged believers to grow in goodness, knowledge and love, and warned about false teachers.
d358-pasture.why: Leadership here means care and example, and Peter, who was once told to feed the sheep, now passes the advice on.

d359-sun_moon.title: Walking in the light
d359-sun_moon.story: In 2 Peter 3 the writer said the Lord is not slow in keeping his promise but is patient, not wanting anyone to perish, and that the day of the Lord will come like a thief. He urged believers to live holy lives and to grow in the grace and knowledge of Jesus. First John 1 to 3 says that God is light, and if we walk in the light as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another. John wrote that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive them, and that we should love not just in words but in action.
d359-sun_moon.why: Walking in the light is about honesty with God and with each other, and it makes room for friendship.

d360-love.title: God is love, and a welcome for travelers
d360-love.story: In 1 John 4 and 5 John wrote, "Beloved, let us love one another, because love comes from God." He said that God is love, and that anyone who loves is born of God and knows God. He wrote that we love because God first loved us, and that if someone says they love God but hates a brother or sister, they do not know God. Second and Third John are two short personal letters. In the third, John praised his friend Gaius for welcoming traveling workers and showing hospitality, and Jude then closes with a short call to keep building on faith.
d360-love.why: Love is described as the clearest mark of knowing God, and welcoming strangers is one way to practice it.

d361-lampstand.title: Seven lampstands
d361-lampstand.story: Revelation 1 says John was on the island of Patmos when, on the Lord's day, he heard a loud voice like a trumpet. He turned and saw seven golden lampstands and, among them, one like a son of man, whose face was like the sun shining at full strength. John fell at his feet as though dead, but he laid his right hand on him and said, "Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last." Chapters 2 and 3 are short letters to seven churches, with praise, correction and encouragement.
d361-lampstand.why: The vision begins with the voice telling John not to be afraid, and the letters show Jesus knows each church closely.

d362-throne.title: The throne room of light
d362-throne.story: John writes that he saw a door standing open in heaven and heard a voice calling him up to see what must happen. He describes a throne with someone seated on it, a rainbow like an emerald around it, flashes of lightning and a sea like glass. Around the throne were twenty-four elders on thrones, and four living creatures who never stop praising. The elders lay their crowns before the throne and say that God is worthy of glory, honor and power, because he created all things.
d362-throne.why: Before the visions of struggle, the book shows worship at the center of everything, with God reigning.

d362-white_robes.title: The throne room of light
d362-white_robes.story: John writes that he saw a door standing open in heaven and heard a voice calling him up to see what must happen. He describes a throne with someone seated on it, a rainbow like an emerald around it, flashes of lightning and a sea like glass. Around the throne were twenty-four elders on thrones, and four living creatures who never stop praising. The elders lay their crowns before the throne and say that God is worthy of glory, honor and power, because he created all things.
d362-white_robes.why: Before the visions of struggle, the book shows worship at the center of everything, with God reigning.

d363-harvest.title: The harvest of the earth
d363-harvest.story: Revelation 10 to 14 is a series of visions John described. John was given a little scroll to eat, which tasted sweet but was bitter in his stomach, and he saw two witnesses who spoke on God's behalf. In chapter 12 he saw a woman clothed with the sun and a great dragon who tried to destroy her child, and a war in heaven. In chapter 14 he saw one like a son of man seated on a cloud with a sharp sickle, and the earth being reaped like a harvest.
d363-harvest.why: Revelation is written in strong pictures, and its main message to readers under pressure is to hold on, because God is in the end the one who gathers the harvest.

d364-ruins.title: The fall of the great city
d364-ruins.story: Revelation 15 describes people standing beside a sea of glass, singing the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb, "Great and wonderful are your works, O Lord God Almighty!" In chapter 16 seven angels pour out bowls of God's judgment on the earth. In chapters 17 and 18, John saw the great city, called Babylon, which had grown rich and proud, fall in a single hour, and the merchants and kings of the earth mourned it. A voice from heaven called God's people to come out of her.
d364-ruins.why: The vision is stark, and at its heart is the claim that proud and unjust power does not last, while God's justice does.

d365-jerusalem.title: The holy city descending
d365-jerusalem.story: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, because the first heaven and earth have passed away. He sees the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven, prepared like a bride dressed for her husband. A loud voice announces that God will make his home among his people and wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death, mourning, crying or pain. The one on the throne says that he is making everything new.
d365-jerusalem.why: The Bible's story ends with God making his home with people and healing what was broken.

d365-rivertree.title: River of life and the tree
d365-rivertree.story: In the last chapter, John is shown a river of the water of life, clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God down the middle of the city's street. On each side of the river stands the tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit, a crop each month, and its leaves are for the healing of the nations. There will be no more curse, and God's servants will see his face. The book closes with an invitation to come and a promise that Jesus is coming soon.
d365-rivertree.why: It echoes the garden of Genesis at the very end, so the Bible opens and closes with a place of life and healing.
